english: “You who are weaned from milk, you who are drawn from the breast, welcome affliction upon affliction, welcome hope upon hope; yet a little, yet a little, because of the scorn of lips, by another tongue” (Isaiah 28:9-11).

You too, then, most God-fearing Ambrose and most devout Protoctetus, are in Isaiah's sense no longer people of the flesh, nor babes “in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1); you have advanced “in” the inward “stature” of your minds (Luke 2:52), and you no longer “need milk” but “solid food” (Hebrews 5:12). So listen, as those “weaned from milk” and “drawn from the breast”, to how, for the weaned, as for athletes, what is prophesied is not a simple affliction but a kind of “affliction upon affliction”. Whoever does not thrust away the affliction “upon affliction”, but welcomes it like a noble athlete, at once welcomes “hope upon hope” as well, and he will enjoy that hope not long after the affliction “upon affliction”. For that is what “yet a little, yet a little” means.
notes_covered: Isaiah 28:9-11 (LXX) set as the epigraph of the whole work
Ambrose and Protoctetus addressed as no longer infants but grown, ready for solid food
The weaned are promised, like athletes, affliction upon affliction
Whoever welcomes the affliction welcomes hope upon hope soon after: 'yet a little'
translator_notes: The Isaiah epigraph follows Origen's Septuagint wording (“welcome affliction upon affliction... because of the scorn of lips”), which differs from the Hebrew-based English text; the citation follows Koetschau's apparatus (Jes. 28, 9-11) and the KJV verse check (weaned from the milk, drawn from the breasts, a little, another tongue).
προσδέχομαι is rendered “welcome” throughout so that Origen's play between Isaiah's command and the athlete who “welcomes” the contest stays visible; it also carries the sense “await”.
title: Weaned athletes welcome affliction upon affliction

english: But even if those who are strangers to the language of the holy Scriptures scorn us and treat us as worthless, calling us either impious or fools, let us remind ourselves that the hope “upon hope”, which is to be given back to us in “yet a little” while, will be given back “because of the scorn of lips, by another tongue” (Isaiah 28:11). And who would not welcome “affliction upon affliction” (Isaiah 28:10) in order at once to welcome “hope upon hope” as well, reckoning with Paul that “the sufferings of the present time”, with which we as it were purchase blessedness, “are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18) from God?

All the more so since “the momentary lightness of our affliction” (it is light, and is called light, for those who are not weighed down by what surrounds them), the more it overflows, the greater and fuller is the “weight of eternal glory” it works for us (2 Corinthians 4:17). That holds if, in the time of those who afflict us and who wish, as it were, to crush our souls, we turn our ruling faculty away from what is painful and look not at the painful things now present but at what is laid up, by the grace of God, for those who have contended “lawfully” in Christ (2 Timothy 2:5), because of their endurance in these things. For God multiplies his benefits, and beyond the worth of the contender's labours he bestows as much as it befits God to give: God who does not count out his gifts meanly, who gives greatly and with understanding enlarges his own graces, upon those who, as far as they were able, have shown by despising the earthen vessel (2 Corinthians 4:7) a love for him with the whole soul.
notes_covered: Scorn from those foreign to Scripture's language fulfils Isaiah's 'scorn of lips, another tongue'
Who would not welcome affliction to gain hope, since present sufferings are nothing to coming glory (Romans 8:18)
Light affliction works an eternal weight of glory if the mind looks past present pain (2 Corinthians 4:17)
God rewards beyond the worth of the labours those who despised the earthen vessel out of love
translator_notes: Origen's wordplay: φαυλίζοιεν (“scorn”) answers Isaiah's φαυλισμὸν χειλέων (“scorn of lips”), and “strangers to the language of the holy Scriptures” answers “by another tongue”; both are kept with the one word “scorn”.
“look not at the painful things now present but at what is laid up” echoes 2 Corinthians 4:18 (look not at the things that are seen); Koetschau does not mark it, so it is left uncited.

Koetschau prints the long sentence “And who would not welcome... the whole soul” with a raised point after “from God” and a full stop at the end; the English keeps Origen's rhetorical question and makes “All the more so since...” a new sentence.
title: Scorned now, rewarded beyond our labours

english: God is loved with the whole soul, I think, by those who, in their great eagerness for communion with God, draw the soul away and set it apart not only from the earthly body but from every body. For them, laying aside “the body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21) comes about without any distraction or being dragged this way and that, whenever the moment allows them, through what is thought to be death, to strip off the body “of death”, and to be heard when they have prayed as the apostle did and said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24).

For who among those who groan “in the tent” (2 Corinthians 5:4) because they are weighed down by the perishable body (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15) will not also give thanks, after first saying, “Who will rescue me from the body of this death?”, when he sees that, rescued through this converse [with God] from “the body of death”, he will in holiness cry out, “Thanks be to God through Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 7:25)?
notes_covered: Whole-souled love draws the soul away from the earthly body and from every body
For such people laying aside the body of humiliation at death comes without inner struggle
Death answers Paul's prayer 'Who will rescue me from the body of this death?' (Romans 7:24)
Those groaning in the tent will give thanks when rescued (Romans 7:25)
translator_notes: “through this converse [with God]”: the Greek has only διὰ τῆς ὁμιλίας, “through the converse (company, intercourse)”. The Patristic Text Archive digitisation of Koetschau confirms ὁμιλίας (not ὁμολογίας, “confession”). The bracket supplies the likely partner from the chapter's opening (“communion with God”) and the prayer just quoted; a reader should weigh it.

Wisdom of Solomon 9:15 (“the perishable body weighs down the soul”) is cited on Koetschau's apparatus (Vgl. Weish. Sal. 9,15), and the wording βαρεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τοῦ φθαρτοῦ σώματος plainly matches; kjv.py cannot print Wisdom.
title: Loving God with the whole soul

english: If anyone finds such a thing hard, he has not “thirsted for God, the mighty, the living” (Psalm 42:2); he has not longed for God “as the deer longs for the springs of water” (Psalm 42:1); nor has he said, “When then shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Psalm 42:2). Nor has he pondered within himself what the prophet pondered when, as “Where is your God?” was said to him “every day” (Psalm 42:3), he poured out “his soul” upon himself, rebuking his soul when, through weakness, it was still growing sorrowful and troubled, and saying: “For I will pass through into the place of the wonderful tent, as far as the house of God, with a voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of one keeping festival” (Psalm 42:4).
notes_covered: Whoever finds this hard has not thirsted for the living God as the deer for water (Psalm 42:1-2)
The prophet, taunted 'Where is your God?', poured out his soul and rebuked its weakness
His answer: he will pass into the wonderful tent, the house of God, with festal joy (Psalm 42:4)
translator_notes: All quotations are from LXX Psalm 41, English Psalm 42; Koetschau's apparatus gives LXX 41:2-5 and 41:11 (= English 42:1-4, 42:10). The taunt “Where is your God?” occurs at 42:3 and 42:10; the citation gives the first.
“the mighty” (τὸν ἰσχυρόν) is in the Septuagint text of the verse Origen quotes, not an addition.
title: The soul that thirsts for God

english: So I prayed that you, throughout the whole of the present contest, would remember the great reward laid up in heaven for those who are persecuted and reviled “for righteousness' sake” (Matthew 5:10) and for the sake of the Son of Man (Luke 6:22), and would rejoice and be glad and leap for joy (Luke 6:23), as the apostles once rejoiced that they had been counted worthy to be dishonoured “for his name” (Acts 5:41). And if ever you feel a shrinking in your soul, let the mind of Christ that is in us say to the soul, when it wishes, as far as lies in its power, to throw that mind into confusion as well: “Why are you so sorrowful, O soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will give thanks to him” (Psalm 42:5); and let it say so again (Psalm 42:11).

Would that the soul were not troubled at all, but that even before the very tribunals, and with bare swords brought down upon the neck, it might be guarded by the peace of God that surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7), and be calm, reckoning that those who are away “from the body” are at home with the Lord of all himself (2 Corinthians 5:8). But if we are not so great as always to keep our calm, then at least let the soul's trouble not pour out or show itself to those outside, so that we may have room to make our defence before God, saying to him, “My God, my soul was troubled within me” (Psalm 42:6).

The Word also urges us to remember what is said in Isaiah in this way: “Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be defeated by their scorn” (Isaiah 51:7). For it is absurd, when God is plainly present over the motion of heaven and of all that is in it, and over everything his divine craft accomplishes on land and sea in the births, structures, nourishment and growth of every kind of animal and plant, to shut our eyes and not look upon God, and to turn our eyes instead to fear of those who will shortly die and be handed over to the judgment they deserve.
notes_covered: Origen prays that Ambrose and Protoctetus remember the reward of the persecuted and rejoice like the apostles
If the soul shrinks, the mind of Christ in us answers it with Psalm 42:5 and its refrain
Ideally the soul stays calm even before tribunals and swords, guarded by God's peace
If not, at least the trouble should not show outwardly, leaving room for a defence before God
Isaiah 51:7: do not fear men's reproach; it is absurd to look away from God to mortal judges
translator_notes: “and let it say so again”: the Greek is only καὶ πάλιν, “and again”. Koetschau's critical note says it refers to the repetition of the Psalm's verse at the close of the psalm (LXX 41:12 = English 42:11), against Delarue's suspicion of a lost quotation; the English supplies the verb from εἰπάτω.
“shut our eyes” (καμμύσαι) may echo Isaiah 6:10 / Matthew 13:15 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited.
“The Word” renders ὁ λόγος, which may mean Scripture's word or the Logos; Origen leaves it open.
title: Rejoicing and calm before the tribunal

english: Abraham was once told by God, “Go out from your land” (Genesis 12:1); and to us, perhaps, it will soon be said, “Go out from the whole earth.” It is good to obey him, so that he may quickly show us the heavens, in which is what is called the kingdom of heaven.

Now one can see that life is full of contests over many virtues, and one can see those who contend in them. For many people other than those of God's portion will be thought to have contended for self-control; some will be thought to have died with courage, holding to their resolve on behalf of their common master; those skilled in arguments that are put to the test, to have cultivated prudence; and those who have set themselves to live justly, to have given themselves to justice. Against each virtue there fights either “the mind of the flesh” (Romans 8:7) or else most of the things outside us. But for piety only “the chosen race, the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9) contends, while the rest of mankind do not show, even in appearance, that if there are forces that fight against the pious, they are resolved to die for piety, preferring death with piety to life with impiety.

Each of those who wish to belong to the chosen race is convinced that he hears God saying at every moment, even when those who are godless under the pretext of having many gods are plotting against him: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exodus 20:3), and “You shall not call to mind the name of other gods in your hearts, nor shall it be named from your mouth” (Exodus 23:13). So by such people God is believed “with the heart unto righteousness” and confessed “with the mouth unto salvation” (Romans 10:10), since they grasp that they will not be justified unless they believe God in this way, with their heart so disposed, nor will they be in salvation unless their word is of the same kind as their disposition.

For those deceive themselves who think that, for attaining the goal in Christ, “for with the heart one believes unto righteousness” is enough, even if “and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation” is not added to it. Indeed one may say that it is more a case of honouring God with the lips while keeping the heart far from him (Isaiah 29:13) than of honouring him with the heart, when the mouth does not confess “unto salvation”.
notes_covered: Abraham was told to leave his land; we may soon be told to leave the whole earth for the heavens
Many outside God's portion contend for self-control, courage, prudence and justice
Only the chosen race contends for piety, ready to die rather than live impiously
God's people hear 'no other gods' at every moment, even under plots
Belief of the heart without confession of the mouth does not reach salvation (Romans 10:10)
translator_notes: “on behalf of their common master” (ὑπὲρ τοῦ κοινοῦ δεσπότου): PTA confirms the wording. Origen is describing people outside God's portion, so the “common master” is most likely a ruler or sovereign served in common; the English keeps the Greek without deciding.

The last sentence (μᾶλλόν ἐστι τοῖς χείλεσι τιμᾶν ... ἤπερ τῇ καρδίᾳ τιμᾶν αὐτόν) can be read two ways: that a silent believer's case is more like lip-honour with a far-off heart than true heart-honour, or (more sharply) that lip-honour is preferable. The English “it is more a case of... than of...” keeps the Greek comparative without choosing; a reader should check.
“God's portion” (τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ μερίδος) may echo Deuteronomy 32:9 or Colossians 1:12 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited.
Romans 8:7 is cited for “the mind of the flesh” fighting against virtue (Koetschau: Vgl. Röm. 8,6f; KJV 8:7 “the carnal mind is enmity”).
title: Only God's chosen people contend for piety

english: If the one who says, “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything” (Exodus 20:4), and what follows, says both “You shall not bow down to them” and “Nor shall you serve them” (Exodus 20:5), as though these differ from each other, then perhaps the one who is devoted to idols serves them, while the one who is not devoted to them, but out of cowardice, which he calls accommodation, makes a pretence towards them so as to seem as pious as the many, does not serve the idols but does bow down to them. And I would say that those who forswear Christianity at the tribunal, or before the tribunal, do not serve the idols but do bow down to them, applying the name of the Lord God, the name “God”, to vain and lifeless matter.

In this way too the people who were defiled “with the daughters of Moab” (Numbers 25:1) bowed down to idols and did not serve them. It is written, in so many words: “They called them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices, and bowed down to their idols, and were initiated into the rites of Baal-Peor” (Numbers 25:2-3). And notice that it is not said, “and they served their idols”. For it was not possible, after so many signs and wonders, for them to be persuaded in a single turn of the moment, by the women with whom they were committing fornication, to think the idols were gods. Perhaps it was in this way too, at the making of the calf in Exodus, that they “bowed down” (Exodus 32:8), without serving the calf, which they had watched being made.

So we must think that the present temptation has come about as a test and a proving of our love for God. “For the Lord will test you”, as it is written in Deuteronomy, “to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul” (Deuteronomy 13:3). But you, when you are tested, “will walk after the Lord your God and fear him and keep his commandments”, above all the one, “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exodus 20:3), “and you will hear his voice and be joined to him” (Deuteronomy 13:4), who takes you from the places here and joins you to himself, into what the apostle called “the growth of God” in him (Colossians 2:19).
notes_covered: The commandment distinguishes bowing down to idols from serving them (Exodus 20:4-5)
The coward who pretends out of 'accommodation' bows down without serving; so do those who forswear Christianity in court
Israel at Baal-Peor bowed down but is not said to have served; likewise perhaps at the golden calf
The present temptation is a test of love for God (Deuteronomy 13:3-4)
translator_notes: “applying the name of the Lord God ... to vain and lifeless matter” may echo Exodus 20:7 (taking the name in vain); Koetschau does not mark it, so it is left uncited.
προστεθήσεσθε / προστιθέντι is a play (“be joined to him ... joins you to himself”); the LXX of Deuteronomy 13:4 has προστεθήσεσθε where the English Bible has “cleave unto him”.
The quotation of Exodus 20:3 is set inside the quotation of Deuteronomy 13:4, as Origen sets it.
title: Bowing down to idols without serving them

english: And if “every evil word is an abomination to the Lord your God”, how great an abomination must we think the evil word of denial to be, and the evil speech that proclaims another god, and the evil oath by the fortune of men, a thing without substance? When this oath is put to us, we must remember the one who taught, “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matthew 5:34). For if the one who swears by heaven offends against the throne of God, and the one who swears by the earth commits impiety, making a god of what is called the footstool of God's feet, and the one who swears by Jerusalem sins, even though it is the city of the great King, and the one who swears by his own head does wrong (Matthew 5:34-36), how great a sin must we think it to swear by someone's fortune? At that time we must also remember the saying, “Of every idle word you will give an account on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). For what other word is as idle as the oath sworn in denial?

But it is likely that the enemy will want to outwit us, by whatever means he can, into bowing down “to the sun or the moon or all the array of heaven”. But we will say that the Word of God “did not command” these things (Deuteronomy 17:3). For we must in no way bow down to created things when the Creator is present, who suffices for all and comes in time to the prayer of all. Not even the sun himself would wish to be bowed down to by those of God's portion, and probably not by anyone else either. Rather, imitating the one who said, “Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God the Father” (Mark 10:18), he would say, as it were, to the one who wishes to bow down to him:

“Why do you call me god? There is one true God. And why do you bow down to me? ‘For you shall bow down to the Lord your God and serve him alone’ (Matthew 4:10). I too am a created being. Why do you want to bow down to one who himself bows down? For I too bow down to God the Father and serve him, and in obedience to his commands I have been subjected to futility because of him who subjected it in hope, and I shall be set free from the bondage of corruption, though I too am now bound to a perishable body, into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:20-21).”
notes_covered: Denial, naming another god and the oath by a man's fortune are abominations worse than any evil word
Christ forbade swearing at all; swearing by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or one's head is already sin (Matthew 5:34-36)
The oath sworn in denial is the idlest word of all (Matthew 12:36)
The enemy may press us to bow to sun, moon and stars, which God did not command (Deuteronomy 17:3)
The sun itself, a creature awaiting freedom, would refuse worship as Christ refused to be called good
translator_notes: “every evil word is an abomination to the Lord your God”: Koetschau compares Proverbs 15:26 and Matthew 12:36; the phrase “an abomination to the Lord your God” is a Deuteronomy formula (e.g. 17:1). No verse gives these words exactly, so the line is left uncited.
“the fortune of men” (τύχη ἀνθρώπων): the oath by a ruler's Fortune demanded of accused Christians; Origen calls fortune “a thing without substance”.
Mark 10:18 is cited (Koetschau: Mark 10:18, Luke 18:19); Origen's wording adds “the Father”, which the Gospel verse does not have.
“bound to a perishable body” may echo 1 Samuel 25:29 or Wisdom of Solomon 9:15 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited.
προσκυνέω is rendered “bow down” throughout, matching chapter VI, where Origen distinguishes it from λατρεύω (“serve”).
title: No oath by fortune, no bowing to creatures

english: We may expect also a certain prophet of impiety, perhaps not one but several, who will speak to us, as the Lord's word, what the Lord did not command (Deuteronomy 18:20), or, as a word of wisdom, what is foreign to wisdom, so that he may kill us with the word of his mouth. But even then, when the sinner stands against us (Psalm 39:1), let us say: “But I, like one deaf, did not hear, and like one mute who does not open his mouth; and I became like a man who does not hear” (Psalm 38:13-14). For deafness to impious words is good, whenever we despair of correcting those who say what is worse.
notes_covered: False prophets of impiety may come, speaking what the Lord did not command, to kill with words
Faced with them, the Christian answers with the deaf and mute man of Psalm 38
Deafness to impious words is right when there is no hope of correcting the speakers
translator_notes: “a [certain] prophet”: the OCR has 'τα ἃ προφήτην'; the PTA digitisation of Koetschau reads τινὰ προφήτην. The singular “prophet” with the plural “not one but several” and the singular “he may kill” are Origen's own.
“as a word of wisdom” may echo 1 Corinthians 12:8 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited because only two words are shared.
“when the sinner stands against us” is the Septuagint wording of LXX Psalm 38:2 (English 39:1, “while the wicked is before me”); not in Koetschau's apparatus but confirmed by the verse text.
Psalm 38:13-14 English = LXX 37:14-15, as Koetschau gives it.
title: Deaf to the prophets of impiety

english: It is useful for us, in times when people are calling us to the opposite course, to consider what God wishes to teach when he says, “I am the Lord your God, a jealous one” (Exodus 20:5). I think that a bridegroom who is turning his bride towards a modest life, one in which she gathers her whole self to the bridegroom and guards in every way against pouring herself out to anyone besides him, would display jealousy even if he is wise, using such a display as a remedy for the bride. In the same way the one who utters the oracle, especially if he proves to be “the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), tells the bride, the soul, that he is a jealous God, drawing his hearers away from all fornication with demons and with those who are thought to be gods.

And it is as a God so jealous that he says of those who have in any way gone whoring after other gods: “They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god; they angered me with their idols. And I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation; with a nation without understanding I will anger them. For a fire has been kindled from my wrath; it will burn to the lowest Hades” (Deuteronomy 32:21-22).
notes_covered: In times of pressure we should ask what God teaches by calling himself jealous
A wise bridegroom shows jealousy as a remedy to keep his bride wholly his
So the Word, the firstborn of creation, calls himself jealous to draw the soul away from demons and false gods
Deuteronomy 32:21-22: God's jealousy burns against those who go after other gods
translator_notes: Origen's wording of Exodus 20:5 here has no second θεός (“I am the Lord your God, jealous”); rendered “a jealous one”.
“the one who utters the oracle” (ὁ χρηματίζων) is the divine speaker of the commandment; Origen suggests it may be the Son, “the firstborn of all creation”.
title: The jealous God and the bride

english: Even if the bridegroom, being wise and free from passion, does not turn his betrothed away from every defilement for his own sake, yet for her sake, seeing her defilement and her abomination, he will do everything that can heal her and turn her back, applying to her, as to a nature with free will, words that turn her away from fornication. What defilement, then, could you conceive worse for a soul than that it should in any way proclaim another god, and not confess the one who is truly the one and only Lord?

I think that, just as “he who is joined to a harlot is one body” (1 Corinthians 6:16), so the one who confesses someone, especially in a time of torture and of testing of faith, is blended and made one with the one he confesses; but the one who denies, by the denial itself, which cuts him off like a sword from the one he denies, suffers division, separated from the one he has denied. So consider whether perhaps it is as a consequence and a necessity, that being confessed befalls the one who confesses and being denied the one who denies, that the saying is spoken: “Whoever confesses in me before men, I too will confess in him before my Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:32).

And the very Word and very Truth might say both to the one who has confessed and to the one who has denied: “With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38). You, then, who measured with the measure of confession towards me, and filled up the measure of confession, will receive a measure of confession from me, shaken, pressed down and running over, which will be given “into your bosom”; and you who measured with the measure of denial, and denied me, will receive, in proportion to the measure of your denial, a measure of my denial of you.
notes_covered: The wise bridegroom heals his betrothed of defilement for her sake, appealing to her free will
No defilement is worse than proclaiming another god and not confessing the one Lord
Confession blends the confessor with Christ; denial cuts him off like a sword
Christ's promise to confess the confessor follows of necessity (Matthew 10:32)
The measure of confession or denial is returned in full (Luke 6:38)
translator_notes: Matthew 10:32 is rendered with Origen's literal “confesses in me ... confess in him” (ὁμολογήσῃ ἐν ἐμοί ... ὁμολογήσω ἐν αὐτῷ), because his point is that confession unites the confessor with Christ.
“filled up the measure” may echo Matthew 23:32 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited. Koetschau notes that MS P and Delarue omit “and filled up the measure of confession”.
“the very Word and very Truth” (ὁ αὐτολόγος καὶ ἡ αὐτοαλήθεια, confirmed by PTA): Christ as Word itself and Truth itself (Koetschau compares John 14:6).
title: Confession unites, denial cuts off

english: How the measure of confession is filled, or is not filled but falls short, we might consider in this way. Suppose that throughout the whole time of examination and temptation we give no place to the devil in our hearts (Ephesians 4:27), when he wishes to defile us with evil thoughts of denial, or of a divided soul, or of some plausible argument that calls us towards what is hostile to martyrdom and to perfection. Suppose, besides, that we do not stain ourselves with even a word foreign to confession, and that we bear all the reproach from our opponents, their mockery and laughter and slander, and the pity with which they think they pity us, when they suppose us to be deluded and foolish and call us misguided. Suppose, further, that we are not dragged about and distracted, by affection for our children or their mother or any of those thought dearest in this life, towards possessions or towards this life, but turn away from all these and become wholly God's, and wholly given to the life with him and beside him, as those who are to share with his Only-begotten and with those who share in him. Then we could say that we have filled up the measure of confession.

But if we fall short even in a single thing, we have not filled up the measure of confession but have defiled it, and mixed into it something foreign to it. So we shall need what those need who have built upon the foundation wood or hay or straw (1 Corinthians 3:12).
notes_covered: The measure of confession is filled only if the devil is given no place in the heart during the trial
No word foreign to confession; all mockery and false pity borne
No pull of love for children, wife, friends, possessions or this life; wholly given to God
Falling short in one thing defiles the measure, like building with wood, hay or straw (1 Corinthians 3:12)
translator_notes: Ephesians 4:27 (“do not give place to the devil”) is not in Koetschau's apparatus, but Origen's μὴ διδοίημεν τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ matches the verse's wording; confirmed with the verse text.

“those who share in him” (τοῖς μετόχοις αὐτοῦ) may echo Hebrews 3:14 or 1:9 (Koetschau: Vgl. Hebr. 3,14); left uncited. “his Only-begotten” may echo John 3:16 / 1 John 4:9 (Koetschau: Vgl.); left uncited.
Chapter XI ends with the 1 Corinthians 3:12 sentence; chapter XII begins with the covenants (Καὶ τοῦτο δὲ ἡμᾶς εἰδέναι χρή).
title: Filling the measure of confession

english: We must also know this: that we received what are called God's covenants on the terms we ourselves agreed with him when we undertook to live as Christians. Among our terms with God was the whole way of life the Gospel sets out, which says: “If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it” (Matthew 16:24-25). And we have often been more deeply inspired on hearing this as well: “For what will a man gain if he wins the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man is about to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each one according to what he has done” (Matthew 16:26-27).

That one must deny oneself, take up one's own cross and follow Jesus is recorded not only by Matthew, whose words we have set out, but also by Luke and Mark. Listen to Luke saying: “He said to all: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his soul will lose it; but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it. For what does a man gain if he wins the whole world but loses or forfeits himself?” (Luke 9:23-25). And to Mark: “And calling the crowd to him together with his disciples, he said to them: If anyone wants to follow after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save his own soul will lose it; but whoever loses it for the sake of the gospel will save it. And what will it profit a man if he wins the whole world and forfeits his soul? For what will a man give in exchange for his soul?” (Mark 8:34-37).

We have long been bound, then, to deny ourselves and to say, “It is no longer I who live” (Galatians 2:20). And now let it be made plain whether we have taken up our own cross and followed Jesus. That has come about if “Christ lives in us”: if, wanting to save our soul so as to receive it back as something better than a soul, we also lose it by martyrdom. For if we lose it for Christ's sake, casting it upon him in the death we die for him, we will win true salvation for it; but if we do the opposite, we will hear that the one who has gained the whole world of the senses at the price of his own ruin, or of having forfeited himself, gains nothing. Once someone has lost his own soul or forfeited it, even if he gains the whole world, he will not be able to give that world “in exchange” for the soul that is being lost. For the soul made “after the image of God” (Genesis 1:27) is more precious than all bodies. One alone has been able to give an exchange for our soul, which before was being lost: he who bought us with his own “precious blood” (1 Peter 1:19).
notes_covered: Baptism as terms agreed with God: the Gospel way of life, deny yourself and take up the cross (Matthew 16:24-27)
The same saying in Luke 9:23-25 and Mark 8:34-37
Losing the soul in martyrdom saves it; nothing can be given in exchange for a soul made in God's image except Christ's precious blood
translator_notes: 'Casting it upon him' (ἐπιρριπτοῦντες) may echo Psalm 55:22 / 1 Peter 5:7 ('cast your care upon him'); not in Koetschau's apparatus, left uncited.
'Christ lives in us' is Galatians 2:20 again; cited once, at 'It is no longer I who live'.
title: The Soul Lost for Christ Is Saved

english: And by certain deeper meanings Isaiah says: “I gave Egypt and Ethiopia and Syene as an exchange for you, since you became precious in my sight” (Isaiah 43:3-4). The exact account of this and of the rest you will know, and very soon, “face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), as friends of the Father and Teacher in heaven, if, as lovers of learning in Christ who want at last to pass beyond learning “through a mirror” and “in a riddle”, you hasten to the one who called you. For friends learn by plain sight and not through riddles, or by a wisdom stripped bare of sounds and words and symbols and types, as they come into touch with the nature of intelligible realities and the beauty of the truth.

If indeed you believe that Paul was caught up “to the third heaven” and “caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words, which a human being is not permitted to speak” (2 Corinthians 12:2, 4), it follows that you will know this: you will at once come to know more and greater things than the unspeakable words then revealed to Paul, after which he came down from the third heaven; and after that knowledge you will not come down, if you take up the cross and follow behind Jesus, whom we have as “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens” (Hebrews 4:14). And you yourselves, not leaving your place behind him, will pass through the heavens, rising above not only the earth and the mysteries of the earth but also the heavens and the things that concern them.

For there are stored up in God sights far greater than these, which no nature of those in a body can take in unless it has first been set free from every body. For I am persuaded that God keeps in store and guards with himself things far greater than those the sun and the moon and the choir of the stars have seen, and greater even than those the holy angels have seen, whom God made “spirit” and “a flame of fire” (Psalm 104:4), so that he may reveal them when the whole “creation” is set free “from slavery to the enemy into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Romans 8:21).
notes_covered: Isaiah 43:3-4 read by a deeper sense: God's exchange for the soul
Lovers of learning who hasten to God will soon know face to face, as friends, beyond the mirror and riddle
Following Jesus the high priest, they will know more than Paul heard in the third heaven and will not come down
Greater sights are stored in God, revealed when creation is set free
translator_notes: 'Learn by plain sight and not through riddles' (ἐν εἴδει καὶ οὐ δι᾽ αἰνιγμάτων) matches Greek Numbers 12:8 word for word; Koetschau does not list it and the KJV wording differs, so it is left uncited (possible allusion).
Romans 8:21 is cited although Koetschau's text (M) reads 'slavery to the enemy' where Paul has 'bondage of corruption' (P and Delarue read τῆς φθορᾶς).
'Spirit' and 'a flame of fire': Koetschau gives Psalm 103:4 LXX (Psalm 104:4) and Hebrews 1:7; Psalm 104:4 cited.
Isaiah 43:3-4 follows the Greek ('Syene'); the KJV has 'Seba'.
title: Following Jesus Through the Heavens

english: And so one of the foremost martyrs, who has a greater love of learning in Christ than many martyrs, will rise further and sooner. But you, holy Ambrose, if you look carefully into a saying of the Gospel, can see that perhaps either no one who has ever lived, or very few, will attain an outpouring of blessedness that is exceptional and greater; and you too will be in such blessedness, if you swim through the contest without wavering. The words run like this. Peter once said to the Saviour: “Look, we have left everything and followed you; what then will there be for us?” (Matthew 19:27). And Jesus said to them (to the apostles, clearly): “Truly I tell you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when God sits on the throne of his glory, you too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left brothers or sisters or parents or children or fields or houses for the sake of my name will receive many times as much and will inherit eternal life” (Matthew 19:28-29).

Because of these sayings I would have prayed, had I acquired as much on earth as you have, or even more, to become a martyr to God in Christ, so that I might receive “many times as much”, or, as Mark says, “a hundredfold” (Mark 10:30). That is far more, since the few things we leave behind, if we are called to martyrdom, are multiplied a hundred times. For this reason, if I bear witness, I would wish to leave children behind too, along with fields and houses, so that with the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Ephesians 3:15), I might be called the father of many times more children, and holier ones, or, to put it precisely, a hundred times more.

If indeed there are fathers, those of whom it was said to Abraham, “But you will go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age” (Genesis 15:15), someone might say (I do not know whether truly) that perhaps those fathers are men who once bore witness and left their children behind, and in return have become fathers of fathers: of the patriarch Abraham and of other patriarchs like him. For it is likely that those who left their children and bore witness become fathers not of infants but of fathers.
notes_covered: A greater love of learning in Christ lifts a martyr higher and sooner
Ambrose may share an exceptional blessedness if he swims through the contest (Matthew 19:27-29)
Origen would wish, were he rich, to leave much and receive a hundredfold, even children (Mark 10:30; Ephesians 3:15)
The fathers of Genesis 15:15 may be martyrs who became fathers of the patriarchs
translator_notes: Crux: Καὶ ἐπέκεινα οὖν τις προμαρτύρων ... τάχιον ἀναβήσεται (M only; P and Delarue omit the sentence). προμάρτυς is rare; taken by analogy with πρόμαχος as 'foremost martyr', with τις + partitive genitive and ἐπέκεινα as an adverb ('further'). Alternatives: 'earlier martyrs', or ἐπέκεινα governing the genitive ('someone beyond the foremost martyrs who have ...'). A human should check.

Origen's text of Matthew 19:28 as printed reads 'when God sits on the throne of his glory' (ὁ θεός), where the Gospel has 'the Son of Man'; translated as printed, no OCR doubt and no note in Koetschau's apparatus.
Origen's wording of Matthew 19:29 has 'parents' and no 'wife' (which chapter 16 relies on); the KJV list includes 'wife'.
The closing sentence on fathers of fathers (εἴπερ δέ εἰσι ... πατέρας) is in M only; P and Delarue omit it.
title: Fathers of Fathers: The Hundredfold Reward

english: But suppose someone, as if “eagerly seeking the greater gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31) and calling blessed the rich martyrs and the martyrs who are fathers, who will beget children a hundredfold and receive fields and houses a hundredfold, asks whether it is reasonable that they, compared with martyrs who were poor in this life, will have their possession among intelligible realities multiplied. We must tell him this. Just as those who endured tortures and pains have shown a more brilliant virtue in martyrdom than those not tested in these things, so too with those who, besides the love of the body and the love of life, have also cut through and burst so many worldly bonds. They have used a great love toward God and have truly taken up the living word of God, which is active and sharper “than any two-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12); and having cut through so many bonds and made themselves wings like an eagle, they have been able to return “to the house” of “the one set over” them (Proverbs 23:5).

It is right, then, that just as those not tested in tortures and pains should yield the first place to those who showed their endurance on racks that wrench the joints, on twisting engines of every kind, and in fire, so also for us who are poor, even if we bear witness, reason prompts us to stand aside from the first place for you, who for the sake of love toward God in Christ trample on the deceitful glory that lays hold of the many, on such great possessions, and on affection for your children.
notes_covered: Objection: why should rich martyrs, who leave more, have their reward multiplied above poor martyrs?
As the tortured outshine the untested, so those who cut so many worldly bonds by love of God outshine others (Hebrews 4:12; Proverbs 23:5)
So the poor, even if martyred, yield first place to Ambrose and Protoctetus
translator_notes: Romans 8:39 (Koetschau 'Vgl.') left uncited: Origen's phrase is the martyr's love toward God in Christ, not God's love.
1 Corinthians 12:31 cited though not in Koetschau's apparatus: ζηλῶν χαρίσματα τὰ μείζονα is Paul's wording.
Proverbs 23:5: wings like an eagle are in both texts; 'returns to the house of the one set over it' is the Greek Proverbs only.
'You' (ὑμῖν) are Ambrose and Protoctetus, the rich addressees; 'us who are poor' is Origen's side.
title: Why Rich Martyrs Take the First Place

english: At the same time, note the dignity of Scripture: it promises brothers and children and parents and fields and houses many times over and a hundred times over, but a wife is not counted along with them. For it is not said, “Everyone who has left brothers or sisters or parents or children or fields or houses or a wife for the sake of my name will receive many times as much.” For “in the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).
notes_covered: Scripture promises a hundredfold of kin, fields and houses but not of a wife, since in the resurrection there is no marrying (Matthew 22:30)
translator_notes: No citation on the saying 'Everyone who has left ... or a wife': Origen quotes it as not written. In the KJV, Matthew 19:29 and Luke 18:29 do list 'wife'; Mark 10:30, the hundredfold promise, does not list it. Origen's own text of Matthew 19:29 (chapter 14) has no 'wife'.
The resurrection saying blends Matthew 22:30 ('in the resurrection') and Mark 12:25 ('the dead', 'the angels in heaven'); Koetschau lists both, Matthew 22:30 cited.
title: Why No Wife Is Promised a Hundredfold

english: What Joshua said to the people when he settled them in the holy land, Scripture might now say to us as well. The passage runs like this: “Now fear the Lord and serve him in uprightness and in righteousness” (Joshua 24:14). And to us, who are being urged to worship idols, it will also say the words that follow, which run like this: “Put away the foreign gods, which your fathers served beyond the river and in Egypt, and serve the Lord” (Joshua 24:14). At the beginning, then, when you were about to be instructed in the faith, it might reasonably have been said to you: “But if it does not please you to serve the Lord, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve, whether the gods of your fathers who lived beyond the river or the gods of the Amorites, among whom you dwell in the land” (Joshua 24:15). And the one instructing you would have said to you: “But I and my house will serve the Lord, for he is holy” (Joshua 24:15).

But now there is no room for these words to be said to you. For then you said: “Far be it from us to forsake the Lord so as to serve other gods. The Lord our God, he is God, who brought us and our fathers up out of Egypt and kept us safe all along the way we travelled” (Joshua 24:16-17). More than that, long ago, in the covenants about godliness, you gave this answer to those who instructed you: “We too will serve the Lord, for he is our God” (Joshua 24:18). If, then, one who breaks covenants made with human beings is a man outside every truce and a stranger to salvation, what must be said of those who by denying set aside the covenants they made with God and run back to Satan, whom they renounced when they were baptized? For against such a case we must say the words Eli spoke to his sons: “If a man truly sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25).
notes_covered: Joshua's charge to Israel in the land (Joshua 24:14-15) is Scripture's word to Christians urged to worship idols
The choice was open before catechesis; at baptism they answered, 'We too will serve the Lord' (Joshua 24:16-18)
Denial breaks the covenant with God and runs back to Satan, renounced at baptism; Eli's warning (1 Samuel 2:25)
translator_notes: Joshua 24:14 'in uprightness and in righteousness' and 24:15 'for he is holy' follow the Greek Joshua; the KJV has 'sincerity and truth' and lacks 'for he is holy'.
1 Samuel 2:25: the Greek first half ('they will pray for him') differs from the KJV ('the judge shall judge him'); the second half matches.
Joshua 24:14 is cited twice because Origen quotes it as two separate sayings.
title: Breaking the Covenant Made at Baptism

english: A great theatre is gathering to watch you as you contend and are called to martyrdom, just as if we were to say that this happens with certain contenders thought to be marvels, when countless thousands gather to see the contest. And when you contend, you will say no less than Paul did: “We have become a theatre to the world, to angels and to human beings” (1 Corinthians 4:9). So the whole world and all the angels, of the right and of the left, and all human beings, both those of God's portion and those of the rest, will hear us as we contend in the contest for Christianity. And either the angels in heaven will rejoice over us, and “the rivers will clap their hands together, and the mountains will exult” (Psalm 98:8), “and all the trees of the field will clap with their branches” (Isaiah 55:12); or, may it not be so, the powers below too, who delight in evil, will rejoice.

There is nothing out of place in seeing, from what is written in Isaiah, the words that those in Hades will speak to the ones who have been defeated and have fallen from the heavenly martyrdom, so that we may shudder all the more at the impiety of denial. For I think that such things will be said to the one who has denied: “Hades below was embittered when it met you; all the giants who ruled the earth rose up together for you, those who raised all the kings of the nations from their thrones. All of them will answer and say to you” (Isaiah 14:9-10). And what will the defeated powers say to the defeated, and those whom the devil has captured to those captured in denial? What, then, are these words? “You too were captured, just as we were, and you were counted among us” (Isaiah 14:10). And if someone who had a great and glorious hope in God is defeated in God through cowardice or through the pains brought on him, he will hear: “Your glory has gone down to Hades, your great gladness; beneath you they will spread decay, and the worm will be your covering” (Isaiah 14:11).

And if someone has often shone in the churches, appearing to them like “the morning star” while his good works shone “before men” (Matthew 5:16), and afterwards, in contending the great contest, has lost the crown of so great a throne, he will hear: “How has the morning star, which rose at dawn, fallen from heaven? He has been crushed upon the earth” (Isaiah 14:12). And this too will be said to him who through denial has become like the devil: “You will be cast out on the mountains, a corpse abhorred, with many dead who were pierced through with swords, going down to Hades. As a garment soaked in blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean” (Isaiah 14:19-20). For how will one be clean who has been defiled with blood and murder, the abominable fall of denial, and steeped in so great an evil?

Now let us show that we have heard the words “He who loves son or daughter above me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). Let us take care that not even a doubt arises in us as to whether we should deny or confess, so that the word of Elijah, which runs like this, may not be spoken to us too: “How long will you go lame on both your knees? If the Lord is God, go after him” (1 Kings 18:21).

title: A Great Theatre Watches the Contest

english: It is likely that we will also be reproached by our neighbours and sneered at by some who surround us and shake their heads at us as at fools. But when this happens, let us say to God: “You have made us a reproach to our neighbours, a sneer and a laughingstock to those around us. You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. All day long my disgrace is before me, and the shame of my face has covered me, at the voice of the one who reproaches and slanders, at the sight of the enemy and the persecutor” (Psalm 44:13-16). And it is a blessed thing, even as all these things are happening, to say to God the words which the prophet, out of his boldness, adds to them: “All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant, and our heart has not turned back” (Psalm 44:17-18).
notes_covered: Expect reproach and mockery from neighbours; answer God with Psalm 44:13-16
Blessed to add the prophet's bold words: we have not forgotten you nor turned back (Psalm 44:17-18)
translator_notes: Koetschau prints M here. title: Mocked by Neighbours, Faithful to God

english: Let us remember that, while we are in this life and perceive the ways that lie outside this life, we say to God: “You have turned our paths aside from your way” (Psalm 44:18). Now is the time to recall that this region, in which we have been brought low, is a place of affliction for the soul, so that in prayer we may say: “For you brought us low in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us” (Psalm 44:19). And with confidence we also say: “If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god, will not God search this out?” (Psalm 44:20-21).
notes_covered: Knowing the ways beyond this life, we confess God turned our paths from his way (Psalm 44:18)
This world is a place of the soul's affliction (Psalm 44:19); we pray boldly that God searches out any idolatry (Psalm 44:20-21)
translator_notes: Psalm 44:18: the Greek Psalter reads 'you have turned our paths aside from your way', the Hebrew (KJV) 'neither have our steps declined from thy way'. Citation kept because it is the verse Origen quotes; his wording is translated.
Psalm 44:19: the Greek 'a place of affliction' corresponds to the KJV 'place of dragons'.
title: This Life as a Place of Affliction

english: Let us strive to take up perfectly not only the martyrdom that is in the open but also the one that is in secret, so that we too may cry out with the apostle: “For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience, that in holiness and the sincerity of God we have conducted ourselves in the world” (2 Corinthians 1:12). And to the apostle's word let us join the prophet's: “But he knows the secrets of the heart” (Psalm 44:21), our heart, and above all if we are being led away to death. Then we will say to God the words that martyrs alone speak: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been counted as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 44:22). And if ever, out of the mind “of the flesh” (Romans 8:6), fear of the judges who threaten us with death steals into us, then let us say to them the word from Proverbs: “Son, honour the Lord and you will be strong, and besides him fear no other.”
notes_covered: Take up the hidden martyrdom of conscience as well as the open one (2 Corinthians 1:12)
God knows the heart's secrets, above all on the way to death; the martyrs' word (Psalm 44:21-22)
Against fear of the judges: 'Son, honour the Lord ... besides him fear no other' (Greek Proverbs 7:1)
translator_notes: 'Son, honour the Lord and you will be strong, and besides him fear no other' is in the Greek Proverbs only (LXX 7:1a, which Koetschau gives as Prov. 7,1); the KJV Proverbs 7:1 differs, so it is left uncited.

title: The Hidden Martyrdom of Conscience

english: This too is useful for our subject. Solomon says in Ecclesiastes, “I praised all the dead above the living, as many as are alive until now” (Ecclesiastes 4:2). Who among the dead could be praised with such good reason as the one who, of his own free choice, accepted death for the sake of godliness? Such a man was Eleazar, who welcomed “death with glory rather than life with defilement” and of his own free will went forward to the rack (2 Maccabees 6:19); or the man who, “taking up a noble resolve worthy of his ninety years, of the eminence of his old age, of his hard-won and distinguished grey hair, of his excellent upbringing from childhood, and still more of the holy legislation established by God” (2 Maccabees 6:23), said:

“It is not worthy of our age to pretend, so that many of the young, supposing that Eleazar at ninety had gone over to foreign ways, should themselves be led astray through me, because of my pretence and for the sake of a brief and fleeting life, while I bring defilement and disgrace on my old age. For even if for the present I escape the punishment that comes from men, I shall not escape the hands of the Almighty, whether alive or dead. So by giving up my life bravely now I shall show myself worthy of my old age, and I shall leave to the young a noble example of how to die a good death, readily and nobly, for the revered and holy laws” (2 Maccabees 6:24-28).

I pray that you, when you come to the doors of death, or rather of freedom, and especially if tortures are brought to bear on you (for there is nothing you can rule out suffering at the will of the hostile powers), may say words like these: “To the Lord, who has holy knowledge, it is plain that, though I could be released from death, I endure harsh pains in my body under the scourge, but in my soul I suffer these things gladly because of my fear of him” (2 Maccabees 6:30). Such, indeed, was Eleazar's death that it was said of him at the last: “Not only to the young but to the greater part of the nation he left his own death as an example of nobility and a memorial of virtue” (2 Maccabees 6:31).

Eleazar chose glorious death over defiled life (2 Macc 6:19, 23)
Eleazar's speech against pretence for the young (2 Macc 6:24-28)
Prayer that the readers speak like Eleazar at the doors of death, or rather of freedom (2 Macc 6:30)
Eleazar's death left as a memorial of virtue (2 Macc 6:31)
translator_notes: Origen quotes 2 Maccabees 6 closely; the English follows his Greek, which differs in small points from the printed Septuagint (ἀνατροφῆς for ἀναστροφῆς; εὐθανατίζειν for ἀπευθανατίζειν; προάγων for προσῆγεν).
title: Eleazar chooses death over pretence

english: The seven brothers too, recorded in the books of the Maccabees, whom Antiochus tormented “with whips and cords” (2 Maccabees 7:1) as they held fast to the worship of God, can be a most beautiful example of strong martyrdom to everyone who stops to consider whether he means to fall short of mere boys. They endured tortures not only one by one, but by having watched the torment of their brothers they also showed a vigorous steadfastness of godliness. One of them, who had become, as Scripture calls him, their “spokesman”, said to the tyrant: “What are you going to ask and learn? For we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers” (2 Maccabees 7:2).

What need is there to tell what they endured when pans and cauldrons were heated red-hot so that they might be tortured in them, each of them having first suffered different torments? The one named their spokesman first had his tongue cut out; then he was scalped, and he bore the scalping as others bear circumcision for the sake of the divine law, thinking that in this too he was fulfilling the word of God's covenant. Not content even with this, Antiochus cut off his extremities “while the rest of the brothers and the mother looked on” (2 Maccabees 7:4), punishing the brothers and the mother with the sight and supposing that by things thought so fearful he would shake their resolve. And so Antiochus, still not satisfied, ordered that the man, made useless in the frame of his body by what he had first inflicted, should be brought still breathing to the fire beneath the pans and cauldrons and fried (2 Maccabees 7:5).

As the vapour rose from the flesh of the most noble athlete of godliness, roasted by the tyrant's cruelty, the rest “urged one another, with their mother, to die nobly”, comforting themselves with the thought that God was watching these things. For the conviction that the eye of God is present to those who endure was enough to give them endurance. And the president of the games for the athletes of godliness encouraged them, being himself comforted and, if I may call it so, gladdened over those who rose up against such great pains. It would be fitting for us too, when we find ourselves in such straits, to say to one another the words they used, which run like this: “The Lord God is watching, and truly he takes comfort in us” (2 Maccabees 7:6).
notes_covered: The seven brothers as a pattern for anyone unwilling to fall short of boys (2 Macc 7:1)
The spokesman: ready to die rather than transgress (2 Macc 7:2)
Tongue cut out, scalping borne like circumcision, mutilation before the family (2 Macc 7:4)
Fried alive in the pan (2 Macc 7:5)
The rest urge one another; God's eye present; God comforted and gladdened (2 Macc 7:5-6)

title: The first brother and God's watching eye

english: When the first had been tested in this way, as gold is tested in a furnace (Wisdom of Solomon 3:6), the second was led off “to be mocked” (2 Maccabees 7:7). The servants of the tyrant's cruelty “tore off his skin with the hair” and called on the sufferer to change his mind, asking whether he would eat food offered to idols “before his body was punished limb by limb”. When he refused to change his mind, he was led to “the next” torture, keeping his resolve to his last breath. For he was not broken in the least and did not give way to the pains, but said this to the ungodly man: “You rather, you accursed wretch, are releasing us from this present life; but the King of the world will raise us up, who die for his laws, to an everlasting renewal of life” (2 Maccabees 7:9).
notes_covered: First brother tested like gold in a furnace (Wis 3:6)
Second brother scalped and urged to eat idol food (2 Macc 7:7)
He refuses and keeps his stand to the last breath (2 Macc 7:8)
The King of the world will raise us to everlasting life (2 Macc 7:9)
translator_notes: Koetschau also names Proverbs 17:3 beside Wisdom of Solomon 3:6 for 'tested as gold'; the word χωνευτήριον matches Wisdom of Solomon 3:6, so only that is cited.
Origen's 'food offered to idols' (εἰδωλόθυτα) is his own word; 2 Macc 7:7 only asks 'will you eat'.
title: The second brother looks to resurrection

english: The third, too, counted his pains as nothing and trampled on them for love of God. “When asked for his tongue, he quickly put it out, and he boldly stretched out his hands” (2 Maccabees 7:10), and he said: “I give these up for the sake of God's laws, and I hope to receive them back from God in such a form as God would give back to those who contend in godliness toward him.”

In the same way the fourth was tortured, bearing the torments and saying that it is better, when departing this life at the hands of men, to wait for the hopes that come from God and to be raised up by him, with a resurrection to which the tyrant will not rise. For he will rise not “to life” (2 Maccabees 7:14) but to reproach and to everlasting shame (Daniel 12:2).

Next he tormented the fifth, who looked straight at Antiochus and reproached him with being mortal, since he did not curb his arrogance but thought a tyranny of a few days to be great power. Even in these torments he declared that his nation had not been “forsaken” by God, who was very soon to torment Antiochus “and his seed” (2 Maccabees 7:16-17).

After him the sixth, at the point of death, said: “Do not deceive yourself. We are paying the penalty for our own sins, so that we may be cleansed in our pains, and we suffer these things willingly” (2 Maccabees 7:18). And he told him that he must not think he would go unpunished when he set himself “to fight against God” (2 Maccabees 7:19). For whoever fights against those made divine by the Word is a fighter against God.
notes_covered: Third brother offers tongue and hands, hoping to receive them back (2 Macc 7:10-11)
Fourth: resurrection from God; the tyrant rises to shame (2 Macc 7:14; Dan 12:2)
Fifth rebukes the mortal tyrant; God will torment him and his seed (2 Macc 7:16-17)
Sixth: we suffer for our sins to be cleansed; do not fight against God (2 Macc 7:18-19)
Those made divine by the Word: to fight them is to fight God
translator_notes: Crux for a human reader: μὴ κολούων αὐτοῦ τὴν ὑπερηφανίαν. The participle is masculine nominative (the fifth brother) but the sense requires Antiochus' arrogance; the English takes it with the king. Variants: κολλούων (P, Delarue), καλλύνων (Wettstein conj.).
Daniel 12:2 is not in Koetschau's apparatus but the wording (εἰς ὀνειδισμὸν καὶ εἰς αἰσχύνην αἰώνιον) is the Greek Daniel 12:2 and KJV confirms the sense; cited inline.
Possible allusion left uncited: Acts 5:39 (θεομάχοι) behind 'fighter against God' (Koetschau, Vgl.). 2 Macc 7:11 and 7:13 are paraphrased only.
title: The third to sixth brothers speak

english: Last of all, Antiochus took the youngest into his hands. Convinced that he too was a brother of those who had counted such great pains as nothing, and that he had the same resolve as they did, he tried other approaches. He thought the boy would be won over by appeals and by assurances given on oath that he would make him rich and “envied” if “he turned from the ways of his fathers”, and that he would be enrolled among his Friends and entrusted with royal “offices” (2 Maccabees 7:24).

But when he achieved nothing at all, since the young man paid no attention to what was said, as being foreign to his own resolve, he “called the mother and urged her to become the boy's counsellor for his safety” (2 Maccabees 7:25). She made a show of being about to persuade her son of what the king wanted, and, mocking the tyrant, she stirred her son with many words about endurance, so that the young man did not wait for the punishment that was coming on him but went ahead of it and called out to the executioners: “Why do you delay and hold back? We obey the law given by God; a command that opposes the divine words must not be accepted.”

Indeed, like a king pronouncing on those who are tried before him, he pronounced judgement against the tyrant, judging him rather than being judged; and he declared that, having lifted up his hands against the heavenly children, he would not escape the judgement of God, the Almighty, who sees all (2 Maccabees 7:34-35).
notes_covered: Antiochus tries oaths and offers on the youngest (2 Macc 7:24)
He calls in the mother as counsellor (2 Macc 7:25)
She feigns compliance, mocks the tyrant, urges endurance (2 Macc 7:26-29)
The boy runs ahead of the torture and calls the executioners (2 Macc 7:30)

title: The youngest brother judges the tyrant

english: Then one could see the mother of so many sons bearing the pains and the deaths of her sons “with good courage because of her hopes in God” (2 Maccabees 7:20). For dews of godliness and a breath of holiness did not let the mother's fire be kindled in her inmost being, the fire that blazes up in many women as at the heaviest of evils.

I think that I have set these things down too, abridging them from Scripture, as most useful for our subject, so that we may see how much power godliness has against the harshest pains and the heaviest tortures, and love for God, which is far stronger than every other love. Human weakness has no share in the citizenship of this love for God: it is driven out of the whole soul as an exile beyond the borders and cannot act even in the least degree, wherever there is someone able to say, “The Lord is my strength and my song” (Psalm 118:14), and “I can do all things in him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus our Lord” (Philippians 4:13; 1 Timothy 1:12).
notes_covered: The mother bears her sons' deaths with courage through hope in God (2 Macc 7:20)
Dew of godliness quenches the mother's fire
Origen abridged the Maccabean story to show the power of love for God
Human weakness exiled from the soul that can say Psalm 118:14 and Philippians 4:13
translator_notes: Possible allusion left uncited: the dew and wind that cooled the furnace in the Prayer of Azariah 26-27 (Daniel 3 Greek additions), behind 'dews of godliness and a breath of holiness' (Koetschau, Vgl.).
The last quotation joins Philippians 4:13 ('in him who strengthens me') and 1 Timothy 1:12 ('Christ Jesus our Lord'); both are cited.
title: Love for God overcomes the mother's anguish

english: What martyrdom is, and how much boldness toward God it brings about, can be learned from this too. The saint, being generous of spirit and wishing to repay the benefits that have come to him from God, asks what he might do for the Lord in return for all that he has received from him; and he finds nothing else that a person of good will could give back to God which would, as it were, balance those benefits, as death in martyrdom does.

For in the hundred and fifteenth Psalm (by the Greek count) the words of the perplexed question are written thus: “What shall I give back to the Lord for all that he has given me?” (Psalm 116:12). And when it has been asked, “What will the one who says this give back to the Lord for all that he has received from him?”, the words of the answer are these: “I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord” (Psalm 116:13).

It is customary to call martyrdom the cup of salvation, as we have found in the Gospel. For when those who wished to sit at the right and at the left of Jesus in his kingdom were reaching for a greater honour, the Lord says to them, “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” (Matthew 20:22), calling martyrdom a cup. This is clear also from the words, “Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me; yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36; Matthew 26:39). But we learn that the one who drinks that cup which Jesus drank will sit with, reign with and judge with the King of those who reign. This, then, is the cup of salvation: whoever takes it will call on the name of the Lord, and “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32).
notes_covered: Martyrdom gives boldness toward God
The saint seeks a return for God's gifts and finds only death in martyrdom
Psalm 116:12-13 read as question and answer
The cup is martyrdom: the sons of Zebedee (Matt 20:22) and Gethsemane (Mark 14:36)
Who drinks Christ's cup sits, reigns and judges with him; calling on the name saves (Joel 2:32)
translator_notes: The wording 'the cup that I drink' (ὃ ἐγὼ πίνω) is Mark 10:38; the setting (right and left 'in your kingdom') is Matthew 20:21-22, which Koetschau names. Cited as Matthew 20:22.
The Gethsemane line blends Mark 14:36 ('take away', 'not what I will, but what you will') with Matthew 26:39 ('if it is possible'); both cited, as Koetschau does.

Possible allusions left uncited: 'King of those who reign' (1 Timothy 6:15); 'reign with' (2 Timothy 2:12). Joel 2:32 is also quoted at Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 (Koetschau lists all three); cited once as Joel 2:32.
title: Martyrdom is the cup of salvation

english: But perhaps someone, because of the words “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39), and without having looked closely at what Scripture means, will think that the Saviour too, as it were, was afraid at the time of his passion. And if he was afraid, someone might say, who is ever brave? But first we will ask those who suppose this about the Saviour whether he was less than the one who says: “The Lord is my light and my Saviour; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers drew near me to eat my flesh, those who afflict me and my enemies themselves grew weak and fell. If an army sets itself in array against me, my heart will not fear; if war rises up against me, in this I will hope” (Psalm 27:1-3).

Perhaps these words spoken in the prophet belong to no one else than the Saviour, who because of the light from the Father and the salvation from him feared no one, and because of the protection with which God shielded him was afraid of nothing. His heart did not fear at all when the whole army of Satan was set in array against him, and his heart, filled with holy teachings, hoped in God when war rose up against him. So it does not belong to the same person to say from cowardice, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and to declare from courage, “If an army sets itself in array against me, my heart will not fear.”

Then let nothing in the passage escape us, and you will notice the word “this”, pointing to the cup, in all three. Matthew recorded the Lord as saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39); Luke, “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me” (Luke 22:42); and Mark, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup away from me” (Mark 14:36).

See, then, whether you can say this. Since every martyrdom, a departure brought about on whatever pretext, is called a cup, the one who said “Let this cup pass from me” was not refusing martyrdom as a kind (for then he would have said, “Let the cup pass from me”), but perhaps this particular form of it. And consider whether it may be that the Saviour, looking into the forms of the cups, if I may call them that, and into what would come about through each, and grasping their differences with a very deep wisdom, declined this form of departure by martyrdom and was quietly asking perhaps for another, heavier one, so that a more universal benefit, reaching more people, might be accomplished through another cup. That was not yet the Father's will to bring about, since he orders things by way and order more wisely than the Son's wish and than what the Saviour saw.

Clearly, in the Psalms the “cup” of “salvation” is the death of the martyrs. That is why “I will take the cup of salvation and call on the name of the Lord” is followed by “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:13, 15). So a “precious” “death” comes to us if we are God's holy ones and not unworthy, so that we die not the common death, if I may call it so, which does nothing for godliness, but a chosen one: the death suffered for Christianity, godliness and holiness.
notes_covered: Gethsemane not cowardice (Ps 27:1-3); triple wording; kinds of cups; heavier cup asked
translator_notes: eide (kinds) of cups: Christ declines this kind, seeks a heavier — kept as Origen's boldest Gethsemane reading.

2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 29). The old English replaced Origen's comparison of the three Gospels with a slash list ('let this pass from me' / 'bear away' / ...), dropped his question to those who think the Saviour was afraid, the reading of Psalm 27 as the Saviour's words, and the Psalm 116 close (alert item 9; mark/SOURCE_ISSUES.md item 1).
title: The Savior’s cup and courage

english: Let us also remember the sins we have committed, and that it is not possible to receive forgiveness of sins without baptism, and that under the laws of the Gospel it is not possible to be baptized a second time with water and the Spirit for the forgiveness of sins, and that the baptism of martyrdom is given to us. For that is what it is called, as is plain from the fact that “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” is followed by “or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark 10:38); and elsewhere it is said, “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how hard pressed I am until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50).

And consider whether the baptism of martyrdom, just as the Saviour's became a cleansing for the world, itself also serves for the healing of many who are being cleansed. For as those who attended the altar under the law of Moses were thought to minister forgiveness of sins to the people of that time through the blood of goats and bulls (Hebrews 9:13), so the souls of “those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus” (Revelation 20:4), who do not attend the altar in heaven in vain, minister forgiveness of sins to those who pray.

At the same time we also know that, just as the high priest Jesus Christ offered himself as a sacrifice, so the priests whose high priest he is offer themselves as a sacrifice; and because of that sacrifice they are seen beside the altar as in their own proper place. But among the priests, those who were without blemish and offered sacrifices without blemish served the Deity, while those marked with the blemishes that Moses recorded in Leviticus (Leviticus 21:17-21) were banished from the altar. And who is the priest without blemish, offering a victim without blemish, if not the one who holds fast to his confession and fulfils every number that the account of martyrdom requires? We have spoken of this earlier.

Martyrs' souls at the heavenly altar minister forgiveness to those who pray (Heb 9:13; Rev 20:4)

translator_notes: Possible allusions left uncited: Acts 2:38 ('for the forgiveness of sins'); Matthew 3:11 and parallels and John 3:5 ('water and the Spirit'); Revelation 6:9 (souls under the altar); 1 Corinthians 9:13 ('those who attend the altar'); Hebrews 7:27, 9:14 (the high priest offering himself without blemish). Koetschau lists these as Vgl.

title: The baptism of martyrdom

english: Let us not be surprised if the blessedness of the martyrs, great as it is, which will be passed in deep peace, calm and fair weather, must begin from a state of things that is thought rather gloomy and, if I may call it so, wintry. For first each of the blessed, travelling the narrow and hard-pressed way (Matthew 7:14) in winter, will have to show the seamanship he has gained, so that afterwards there may come to pass what is said in the Song of Songs to the bride who has swum through the winter: “My beloved answers,” it says, “and says to me: Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove; for see, the winter is past, the rain is gone, it has taken itself away” (Song of Solomon 2:10-11).

And you, keep this in mind as well: you cannot hear the words “The winter is past” unless you fight your way through the present winter with strength and vigour. And after the winter has passed and the rain has gone and taken itself away, the flowers will appear (Song of Solomon 2:12); for “those planted in the house of the Lord will blossom in the courts of our God” (Psalm 92:13).
notes_covered: The martyrs' calm blessedness begins from a wintry, gloomy state
The narrow way in winter tests each one's seamanship (Matt 7:14)
The bride who swam through winter hears 'the winter is past' (Song 2:10-11)
Only those who fight through the present winter hear it; then the flowers (Song 2:12; Ps 92:13)
translator_notes: Psalm 92:13 is LXX Psalm 91:14 (Koetschau 'Psal. 91, 14').
title: Winter comes before the flowers

english: We know this too: once Jesus has persuaded us to abandon idols and the godlessness of many gods, the enemy cannot persuade us to worship idols, but he wants to force us. That is why he works such things against those over whom he gains power, and he will make those who are tested either martyrs or idolaters. Often, even now, he says, “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9). So let us take care that we never worship idols and subject ourselves to demons; for the idols of the nations are demons.

What a thing it is to leave Christ's kindly yoke and his “light” “burden” (Matthew 11:30), and to put oneself once more under a yoke of demons and carry a burden of the heaviest sin, after we have come to know that “the heart” of those who serve idols “is ashes” and “their life is more worthless than clay” (Wisdom of Solomon 15:10), and after we have said, “How false are the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no one among them who sends rain” (Jeremiah 16:19; 14:22)!
notes_covered: The enemy cannot persuade Christians back to idols, so he uses force: martyrs or idolaters
His offer even now: 'All these I will give you' (Matt 4:9)
Idols of the nations are demons
Do not trade Christ's light yoke for the demons' heavy one (Matt 11:30; Wis 15:10; Jer 16:19, 14:22)
translator_notes: 'The idols of the nations are demons' is left uncited: Koetschau names 1 Chronicles 16:26 (Vgl.), and the wording is that of the Greek Psalm 95:5 (English 96:5), but English Bibles from the Hebrew read 'idols', not 'demons', so no English verse says it.
The last quotation joins Jeremiah 16:19 (false idols of our fathers) with Jeremiah 14:22 (none that can send rain); both cited.
title: The enemy forces what he cannot persuade

english: It was not only long ago that Nebuchadnezzar set up the “golden image” (Daniel 3:1), nor only then that he threatened Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael that, if they did not worship, he would throw them “into the furnace of fire” (Daniel 3:6). Even now Nebuchadnezzar says the same things to us, the true Hebrews, those who cross over. But, so that we may know by experience the heavenly dew that quenches every fire from us and cools our ruling mind, let us imitate those holy men. Perhaps even now Haman wants you, the Mordecais, to bow down to him (Esther 3:2); but you, Israel, must say: “I will not set the glory of men above the glory of God.”

Let us overthrow Bel by the word of God and kill the dragon with Daniel, so that, when we come near the mouths of lions, we may be beyond suffering any harm from them, while only those who are to blame for our present contest are devoured by the lions that cannot swallow us. Let us hold fast to this: among the brave deeds of Job this too is spoken: “[If] I laid my hand upon my mouth and kissed it, then let this too be counted to me as the greatest lawlessness” (Job 31:27-28). And it is likely that they will order us to put our hand to our mouth and kiss it.
