Heavenly dew quenches the fire; imitate the three young men
Haman wants the Mordecais to bow; answer 'not the glory of men above God' (Esth 3:2)
Overthrow Bel, kill the dragon with Daniel; the lions devour only the accusers

title: Nebuchadnezzar still demands our worship

english: Let us note this too: the Saviour's prophecies about martyrdom come not in his words to the crowds but in his words to the apostles. For after the passage “These twelve Jesus sent out, charging them, ‘Do not go off on the road of the Gentiles’” (Matthew 10:5), and what follows, there comes: “Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will flog you; and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles. When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak, for what you are to speak will be given you in that hour; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of the Father speaking in you. Brother will hand over brother to death, and father child, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in this city, flee to the other; and if they persecute you out of that one, flee to another. For truly I tell you, you will not finish the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes” (Matthew 10:17-23).

Luke records words of the same kind: “When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not worry about how you will defend yourselves or what you will say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you must say” (Luke 12:11-12). And after other things: “So settle it in your hearts not to rehearse your defence; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of those who oppose you will be able to withstand or contradict. You will be handed over even by parents and brothers and relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death, and you will be hated by all because of my name. And not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance gain your souls” (Luke 21:14-19).

Mark too says the like: “When they lead you away and hand you over, do not worry beforehand or rehearse what you are to speak, but whatever is given you in that hour, speak that; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. Brother will hand over brother to death, and father child, and children will rise up against parents and put them to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name; but the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Mark 13:11-13).

These words too in Matthew, which urge us on to martyrdom, were spoken to none other than the Twelve. We also shall need to hear them, since by hearing them we shall become brothers of the apostles who heard them and shall be counted among the apostles. The sayings run like this: “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew 10:28). And next after these the Lord teaches us that no one comes to the contest of martyrdom without providence. For it is said: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground without the Father who is in heaven. As for you, the hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. Everyone, then, who confesses in me before men, I too will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:29-33).

Equivalent to these are the words in Luke: “I say these things to you, my friends: do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do. But I will show you whom to fear: fear him who, after killing, has authority to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear him. Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? And not one of them is forgotten before God. Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. And I tell you, everyone who confesses in me before men, the Son of Man too will confess in him before the angels of God; but the one who denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God” (Luke 12:4-9). And in another place: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26). Mark too recorded something close to this: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in the adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man too will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of the Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38).

So those who put us to death kill a bodily life; for that is the force of “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body”, a saying given in the very same words by Matthew and by Luke. And after killing the body, even if they want to, they cannot kill the soul; indeed they do not have “anything more to do”. For how could a soul be destroyed that has been made alive by the confession itself? The one who urges us on to martyrdom in Isaiah, and his servant, bear witness to it in return, where it is written: “Become my witnesses, and I am a witness, says the Lord God, and the servant whom I have chosen” (Isaiah 43:10).

Note this too: this command was given not to Jesus' slaves but to his friends: “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that have nothing more they can do” (Luke 12:4). We must therefore fear “him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna”. For he alone, “after killing”, has “authority to cast into Gehenna”. And he will indeed cast into it those who were afraid of those who kill the body and were not afraid of “him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” and of “him who after killing has authority to cast into Gehenna”. If the hairs of anyone's head are numbered, plainly those of the ones beheaded for Jesus' sake are numbered too. We will confess in the Son of God, before men and not before gods, so that the one we confessed may repay us, confessing us before his God and Father, and himself confessing in heaven the one who confessed him on earth.

Parallel warnings in Luke 12:11-12, Luke 21:14-19 and Mark 13:11-13
Hearing these words makes us brothers of the apostles; Matthew 10:28-33 on fear and providence
Luke 12:4-9, Luke 9:26 and Mark 8:38 on confessing and shame
Killers take only bodily life; a soul made alive by confession cannot be destroyed (Isaiah 43:10)
The command is to friends; fear him who can cast into Gehenna; confess in the Son so he confesses us
translator_notes: Origen's Matthew 10:23 has the extra clause “and if they persecute you out of that one, flee to another” (κἂν ἐκ ταύτης διώκωσιν, φεύγετε εἰς τὴν ἄλλην); kept as he quotes it.
Origen's Matthew 10:20 reads “the Spirit of the Father” (no “your”); Luke 12:11 reads φέρωσιν; Mark 8:38 reads “the adulterous” generation (τῇ, not “this”); all kept as quoted.
“confess in me ... confess in him” keeps the Greek ὁμολογεῖν ἐν, because Origen builds on it at the close (“we will confess in the Son of God”) and in ch. 35.

“before men and not before gods” (καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ οὐ θεῶν ἔμπροσθεν) is translated as printed; the point of “not before gods” is not explained in the text and Koetschau notes no variant. A human reader may want to check it.
Repeated short quotations in the last paragraph (Matthew 10:28; Luke 12:5; Matthew 10:30) are not cited again; each was cited at its full quotation above.
The old English attached a quotation of John 15:15 and Mark 13:9-10 that Origen does not quote here; both removed.
title: Christ's warnings to the apostles about persecution

english: Who, reckoning such things, will not utter that saying of the apostle: “The sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18)? For how is the confession before the Father not far greater than the confession before men? And how does the confession in heaven made by the one who was confessed not surpass beyond all measure the confession on earth, by which the martyrs confess the Son of God? But let anyone who reckons on denying “before men” remember the one who said, and does not lie, “I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:33).

Since Matthew wrote, “I too will confess in him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32), and Luke, “The Son of Man too will confess in him before the angels of God” (Luke 12:8), I pause over this: perhaps the “firstborn of all creation”, the “image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), confesses the one who has confessed, before the Father in heaven; while he who came “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3), and for that reason is “Son of Man”, who was born of a woman, she too being human, and for that reason is called “Son of Man”, which is how the man in Jesus is understood, confesses those who have confessed “before the angels of God”. A corresponding account must also be given of those who have denied.

We must consider this further. The one who confesses in the Son “before men” commends, as far as lies in him, Christianity and the Father of this Christianity before those in whose presence he confesses; while the one who is confessed by the firstborn of all creation and by the Son of Man is commended, through the confession of the Son of God and of the Son of Man, to the Father in heaven and to the angels of God. And if indeed “it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (2 Corinthians 10:18), how can we fail to hold that the one judged worthy to be commended to the Father in heaven and to the angels of God is approved? And if he is approved, and those like him, whom the Lord has tested “like gold in a furnace” by tortures and interrogations “and accepted like the whole burnt offering of a sacrifice” (Wisdom of Solomon 3:6), what must we say of those who were exposed in the furnace of temptation and denied, whom he denies as unapproved before the Father in heaven and “before the angels of God” (Luke 12:9), denying the one who deserves denial?
notes_covered: Romans 8:18: present sufferings are nothing beside the coming glory; heavenly confession outweighs earthly
Whoever thinks of denying should remember Christ's promise to deny him
Matthew's 'before the Father' and Luke's 'before the angels': perhaps the firstborn and the Son of Man confess at two levels
The confessor commends Christianity before men; the confessed is commended before the Father and angels (2 Corinthians 10:18)
The approved are tried like gold (Wisdom of Solomon 3:6); the deniers are disowned as unapproved
translator_notes: Possible allusions left uncited: “born of a woman” (Galatians 4:4; Koetschau gives Vgl. Matthew 1:20 and John 5:27 for this line); “image of the invisible God” also recalls 2 Corinthians 4:4 and Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 (Koetschau); “furnace” recalls Daniel 3:6 and Matthew 13:42, 50 (Koetschau, Vgl.).
Wisdom of Solomon 3:6 is cited because Koetschau's apparatus names it and Origen's words match the Septuagint verse word for word (ὡς χρυσὸν ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ ... ὡς ὁλοκάρπωμα θυσίας προσεδέξατο).
“the Father of this Christianity” (τὸν πατέρα τοῦ χριστιανισμοῦ τούτου) is taken as God the Father, matching “the Father in heaven” in the next clause.
title: Confessed before the Father and the angels

english: And we must struggle not only against denying, but also against being ashamed in the least when those who are strangers to God think that we suffer things that deserve shame. Above all so, holy Ambrose, if, glorified and welcomed by so very many cities, you are now walking as it were in a procession, carrying the cross of Jesus and following him as he leads you before governors and kings, so that he himself, journeying with you, may himself give a mouth and wisdom to you, and to you also, Protoctetus, his fellow contestant, and to those who bear witness with you, who are filling up “what is lacking” of the sufferings “of Christ” (Colossians 1:24); and so that he may come with you to the paradise of God, showing how you may pass through “the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns and guards the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24).

For even if both of these guard “the way of the tree of life”, they guard it so that no unworthy person may be allowed to pass along it and come to the tree of life. The flaming sword will hold back those who have built upon the foundation that is laid, Jesus Christ, “wood or hay or straw” (1 Corinthians 3:12), and the most combustible wood, the one that burns longest, the wood, if I may call it so, of denial. But the cherubim will receive those who by their nature cannot be held by the flaming sword, because they have built nothing akin to it, and will escort them to “the tree of life” and to all that “God planted” in the east and “made to spring up” “out of the earth” (Genesis 2:8-9).

With Jesus journeying with you to paradise, despise the serpent, conquered and crushed under the feet of Jesus and, through him, under yours as well, since he has given you “authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, so that none of them may harm you” (Luke 10:19).
notes_covered: Struggle not only against denial but against shame before outsiders
Address to Ambrose in procession with the cross, and to Protoctetus, filling up Christ's sufferings
Jesus leads them past the cherubim and flaming sword to the tree of life
The sword holds back those who built wood, hay, straw and the wood of denial; the cherubim escort the rest
Despise the serpent crushed under Jesus' feet and theirs (Luke 10:19)
translator_notes: Possible allusions left uncited: taking up the cross (Matthew 16:24, Mark 8:34, Luke 9:23, Koetschau Vgl.); the paradise of God (Luke 23:43, Vgl.); the serpent crushed under feet (Romans 16:20, Vgl.); “a mouth and wisdom” recalls Luke 21:15 and “before governors and kings” Matthew 10:18 (both quoted in ch. 34).
ξύλον means both “wood” and “tree”; Origen sets the “wood of denial” against the “tree of life”. The English uses “wood” for the building material and “tree” for the tree of life.

Koetschau prints “Gen. 3, 8. 9” for the planting clause in this scan; the words quoted (ἐφύτευσεν ὁ θεὸς ... ἐν ταῖς ἀνατολαῖς ... ἐξανέτειλεν ἐκ τῆς γῆς) are Genesis 2:8-9, confirmed by text; the 3 is taken as an OCR misreading of 2.
OCR: “αὐτός ὅσοι καὶ δῷ” is read as αὐτός σοι καὶ δῷ (“may himself also give you”), the σοι of the line before repeated; no word is supplied.
title: Past the flaming sword into paradise

english: So we must neither deny the Son of God nor be ashamed of him, or of his own people, or of his words. We must listen to this: “Whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:33); and to this: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of mine, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels” (Luke 9:26); and to this: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in the adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man too will be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of the Father with the holy angels” (Mark 8:38).

Jesus too once “endured a cross, despising shame”, and for this reason “sat down at the right hand” of God (Hebrews 12:2). His imitators too, despising shame, will sit with him and reign with him in heaven: with him who came to cast peace not “on the earth” but on the soul of his own disciples, and to cast “a sword” “on the earth” (Matthew 10:34). For since “the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing as far as the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12), this Word now above all bestows on our souls the peace that surpasses all understanding (Philippians 4:7), which he left to his apostles (John 14:27); but he has cast a sword between the image of the earthy one and that of the heavenly one (1 Corinthians 15:49), so that, taking to himself for the present the heavenly one in us, he may later, when we have become worthy not to be cut in two, make us wholly heavenly.

He came to cast not only “a sword” “on the earth”, but also “fire”, of which he says, “How I wish it were already kindled!” (Luke 12:49). So let this fire be kindled in you too, wiping out every earthly and body-loving thought of yours; and be baptized now, with all eagerness, with the baptism by which Jesus “was hard pressed until it was accomplished” (Luke 12:50).

And you who have “a wife and children and brothers and sisters”, remember: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26). And both of you, remember: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate”, besides the former, “his own soul as well, he cannot be my disciple”. But hate your own soul in such a way that by hating it you keep it for eternal life. “For the one who hates”, he says, “his own soul in this world keeps it for eternal life” (John 12:25). So hate your soul for the sake of eternal life, persuaded that the hatred Jesus teaches you to hate with is good and profitable. And just as we shall have to hate the soul so that it may be kept for eternal life, so you who have them, hate “wife and children and brothers and sisters”, so that you may benefit those you hate: through the very fact of having hated them you gain boldness to do them good, once you have become a friend of God.
notes_covered: Neither deny nor be ashamed of the Son, his own or his words (Matthew 10:33; Luke 9:26; Mark 8:38)
Jesus despised shame and sits at God's right; his imitators will reign with him
Christ gives peace to souls but casts a sword between the earthy and heavenly image (Hebrews 4:12)
Let the fire of Luke 12:49 burn away earthly thoughts; accept the baptism of martyrdom
Hate family and even one's soul for eternal life, a good hatred that lets the martyr help those he leaves
translator_notes: Origen's Luke 9:26 here reads “me and mine” (με καὶ τοὺς ἐμούς, without “words”), which matches his “his own people” in the first sentence; kept. In ch. 34 the same verse has “my words”.
Possible allusions left uncited: reigning with him (2 Timothy 2:12, Koetschau Vgl.); sitting at the right hand (Hebrews 8:1, Vgl.); “cut in two” (Luke 12:46, Vgl.).
“his own soul” (ψυχή) is kept as “soul” rather than “life” so that Origen's play on hating the soul to keep it for eternal life, and the soul that cannot be killed in ch. 34, stay visible.
“you who have a wife and children” addresses Ambrose (singular σύ); “both of you” (ἀμφότεροι) adds Protoctetus.
title: The sword, the fire and a good hatred

english: At the same time, remember also the one who prayed in the Spirit about the children of martyrs, left behind because of their love for God, and said: “Preserve the sons of those who have been put to death” (Psalm 79:11). Only know that “it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God” (Romans 9:8); and that, just as it is said to those of the seed of Abraham, “I know that you are the seed of Abraham” (John 8:37), and “If you were children of Abraham, you would be doing the works of Abraham” (John 8:39), so it will also be said to your children: I know that you are the seed of Ambrose; and: if you are children of Ambrose, you do the works of Ambrose.

And perhaps they will do them, since you will benefit them more after such a departure than if you stayed with them. For then you will love them with more knowledge and pray for them with more understanding, if [you learn] that they are your children and not only your seed. Keep this on your lips now: “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37), and this: “Whoever finds his soul will lose it, and whoever loses his soul for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39).
notes_covered: The Psalm's prayer for the sons of the slain covers martyrs' children (Psalm 79:11)
True children are known by deeds, as with Abraham's seed; so with Ambrose's children
A martyr's departure may help his children more than his presence
Matthew 10:37 and 10:39 to keep on the lips
translator_notes: OCR crux: “ἐὰν nass. ὅτι” cannot be read; a verb of knowing or seeing is needed before ὅτι. English gives “if [you learn] that”. A human should check Koetschau's print (p. 36, line 7).
Psalm 79:11 (LXX 78:11) is cited from Koetschau's apparatus (Psal. 78, 11); the Septuagint has “the sons of those put to death” where the Hebrew-based English has “those appointed to die”.
“you do the works of Ambrose” (ποιεῖτε) could also be read as a command (“do the works of Ambrose”); the indicative is kept because the next sentence says “perhaps they will do them”.
Origen quotes only the son-or-daughter half of Matthew 10:37; the old English added the father-or-mother half and Matthew 10:38, which are not in his text here.
title: Leaving children behind for Christ

english: By your eagerness for martyrdom give room to the Spirit of your Father, who speaks in those handed over for their godliness (Matthew 10:20). If you see yourselves hated and loathed and thought to be ungodly, then take up the words, “Because of this the world hates you,” “because you are not of this world”; “if you were of this world, the world would love its own” (John 15:19). You have borne many reproaches for Christ's sake and many dangers since you came to believe: go forward in endurance to the end, since “he who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). Know that, as Peter says, you will rejoice, “though now for a little while, if need be, you have been grieved by various trials, so that the proof of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire, may be found to praise and glory and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:6-7). But hear “grieved” in the sense of “having laboured”, as is clear also from “In grief you will bear children” (Genesis 3:16); for a woman does not always give birth in grief at what she suffers, but in labour.

If the saying is useful to Christ's disciples, “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes and the pride of life, is not of the Father but is of the world. And the world is passing away, and its lust” (1 John 2:15-17), then do not love the things that pass away. Do the will of God and become worthy to be one with the Son and the Father and the Holy Spirit, according to the Saviour's prayer, when he says, “As I and you are one, that they also may be one in us” (John 17:21-22). And how many days can a man gain by loving “the world” or “the things in the world” while he loses or destroys his own soul and carries about a conscience weighed down beyond “a heavy burden” (Psalm 38:4), weighed down by the fall of denial? Let each of us remember how often he has been in danger of dying the common death, and let us consider whether we may not have been kept for this: that, baptized in our own blood and washed of every sin, we may pass our days beside the altar in heaven with those who have contended alongside us.
notes_covered: Spirit speaking (Mt 10:20); world-hate (Jn 15:18-19); gold (1 Pet 1:6-7); Gen 3:16 pains; 1 Jn 2:15-17; Jn 17:21; blood-baptism
added_allusions: Matthew 16:26 (possible: gaining the world, losing the soul)
translator_notes: 2026-11-11: retranslated in full from Koetschau (GCS 2, ch. 39); the old English was a digest ('Take pattern through preparation unto martyrdom...'). The locked source block had lost one line of the GCS page (line 25, 'γὰρ πάντως ἐν λύπῃ τῷ πάϑει τίκτει γυνὴ ἀλλὰ ἐν πόνῳ'); restored from sources/gcs2_martyrium_slice.txt and translated. 'εἰ μὲν χρήσιμον τοῖς Χριστοῦ μαϑηταῖς τό' is in M only (P and Delarue omit it); English follows Koetschau's text.
title: The Spirit speaks through the willing

english: But suppose someone gives way, from a great love of life, or from softness in the face of hardship, or from the arguments, thought persuasive, that are put to us by those who try to win us over to the worse course, and denies that there is one God and his Christ, and confesses demons or Fortunes. Let such a man know that he is preparing “a table for the demon” and filling “a mixed cup for Fortune”, that he has forsaken the Lord and is forgetting his holy mountain, and that he will be liable to these reproofs, which Isaiah wrote down in this way: “But you who have forsaken me and are forgetting my holy mountain, who prepare a table for the demon and fill a mixed cup for Fortune, I will hand you over to the sword; you will all fall in the slaughter. For I called you and you did not answer; I spoke and you paid no heed; you did what was evil before me and chose what I did not want. Therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: See, those who serve me will eat, but you will go hungry; see, those who serve me will drink, but you will be thirsty; see, those who serve me will be glad, but you will be put to shame; see, those who serve me will exult with gladness, but you will cry out for pain of heart and wail for a crushed spirit. For you will leave my name to my chosen ones for their fill, but the Lord will destroy you” (Isaiah 65:11-15).

Again, if we understand what the Lord's table is and want to share in it, let us recognise the words, “You cannot share in the Lord's table and in a table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). And if we understand what is meant by “I will not drink from now on of this fruit of the vine until that day, until I drink it new in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 26:29), and wish to be found among those who drink with Jesus, let us heed the words, “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and a cup of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). Who, hearing John, the son of thunder, say, “He who denies the Father and the Son: everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either; he who confesses the Son has the Father also” (1 John 2:22-23), will not be afraid to deny the Son by saying he is not a Christian, when by denying him he will not have the Father? And who would not be moved to confess that he is a Christian, in deeds and in words, so that he may have the Father as well? For those who confess have the Father.
notes_covered: Denial from love of life, softness or persuasion is setting a table for the demon and a cup for Fortune (Isaiah 65:11-15 quoted in full)
One cannot share the Lord's table and cup and the demons' (1 Corinthians 10:21; Matthew 26:29)
John, son of thunder: denying the Son loses the Father; confessing in deed and word keeps him (1 John 2:22-23)
translator_notes: 'τάδε λέγει λέγει κύριος κύριος' is M's reading, which Koetschau prints (P and Delarue: 'λέγει κύριος'); the doubled 'λέγει' looks like dittography and is rendered once; 'κύριος κύριος' is kept as 'the Lord, the Lord'.
Isaiah 65:15 in Origen's text reads 'my name' (τὸ ὄνομά μου) and 'for satiety' (εἰς πλησμονήν, the LXX rendering); English follows Origen's text, not the Hebrew ('your name for a curse').
'the son of thunder' alludes to Mark 3:17 (Boanerges); left uncited inline because it is a title, not a quoted clause.
Koetschau's apparatus marks 'ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ θέλομεν ... ποτήριον δαιμονίων' and the opening words of the 1 John quotation as missing in P and Delarue; English follows Koetschau's text (M).
title: No sharing the Lord's table and the demons'

english: If we have passed “from death to life” (1 John 3:14) by passing from unbelief to faith, let us not be surprised if the world hates us (1 John 3:13). For no one who has not passed “from death to life”, but remains in death, can love those who have moved out of the dark house of death, if I may call it that, into the buildings made of living stones (1 Peter 2:5) and filled with the light of life. Jesus “laid down his life for us” (1 John 3:16); let us, then, lay down ours as well. I will not say for his sake, but for our own, and also, I think, for those who will be built up by our martyrdom.

A time for boasting has come upon us Christians. For, he says, “not only so, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance, and endurance proven character, and proven character hope; and hope does not put us to shame” (Romans 5:3-5). Only let “the love of God” be poured out “in our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Romans 5:5). Let Paul say, “If, humanly speaking, I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus” (1 Corinthians 15:32); and let us say, “If, humanly speaking, I was put to death in Germany.”
notes_covered: Passed from death to life through faith, we should not wonder that the world hates us (1 John 3:13-14)
Those in death cannot love those who have moved into the house of living stones and the light of life
Jesus laid down his life for us; we lay down ours, for ourselves and for those built up by our martyrdom (1 John 3:16)
A time to boast in afflictions (Romans 5:3-5); Paul's beasts at Ephesus and our death in Germany (1 Corinthians 15:32)
translator_notes: Crux: 'ἡμεῖς δὲ «εἰ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον» ἀνῃρέθην ἐν Γερμανίᾳ' has a plural subject ('we') with a first-person singular aorist ('I was killed'), matching Paul's singular. Koetschau prints it without emendation and the English follows it as printed, supplying 'let us say' from 'λεγέτω'. Why Germany is named is not explained in the text; a link to events on the German frontier at the time of writing has been suggested but is unverified here. A human should look at this line.

Koetschau's apparatus gives John 5:24 for 'from death to life' and John 15:18 for the world's hatred; the wording (first person plural 'μεταβεβήκαμεν', 'μὴ θαυμάζωμεν ... εἰ μισεῖ') matches 1 John 3:13-14 more closely, which is what is cited inline.
'φωτὸς ζωῆς' ('light of life') may echo John 8:12; left uncited.
Romans 5:5 is quoted in two pieces ('ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ' ... 'ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ἡμῶν διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου') with Origen's own 'μόνον ... ἐκκεχύσθω' ('only let it be poured out') between them.
title: From death to life, and a time to boast

english: If “as the sufferings of Christ abound, so through Christ comfort also abounds” (2 Corinthians 1:5), let us welcome the sufferings of Christ with the greatest eagerness, and let them abound in us, if we really long for abundant comfort, the comfort with which all who “mourn” “will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4), though perhaps not equally. For if the comfort were equal, it would not have been written, “As the sufferings of Christ abound towards us, so our comfort also abounds.” Those who share in the sufferings will share in the comfort too, in proportion to the sufferings they share with Christ. You learn this also from the one who speaks of such things as a man entrusted with them: “For we know that as you share in the sufferings, so also in the comfort” (2 Corinthians 1:7). And God says through the prophet, “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). What other time, then, is so acceptable as when, for our godliness towards God in Christ, we are led away under guard, paraded through the world, triumphing rather than being led in triumph? For the martyrs in Christ strip off with him “the principalities and the powers” (Colossians 2:15) and share his triumph: as they come to share in his sufferings, so they share also in the valiant deeds done in his sufferings. Among these is the triumph over “the principalities and the powers”, which in a little while you will see conquered and put to shame. What other day is so truly a day of salvation as the day of such a release of ours from this place?

But I urge you: “give no offence in anything”, so that the presbyterate or “the ministry” “may not be discredited” through you, “but in everything commend yourselves as ministers of God, in much endurance” (2 Corinthians 6:3-4), saying, “And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?” (Psalm 39:7); “in afflictions”, persuaded that “many are the afflictions of the righteous” (Psalm 34:19); “in necessities”, so that we may claim blessedness as our necessity; “in straits”, so that, travelling the strait and hard-pressed way without leaving any of it untrodden, we may come through to life (Matthew 7:14). If need be, let us commend ourselves also “in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labours, in sleepless nights, in fastings” (2 Corinthians 6:5). For see, the Lord, and “his reward” in his hand, “to repay each one” as his works are (Revelation 22:12).
notes_covered: Comfort abounds in proportion to the share in Christ's sufferings (2 Corinthians 1:5, 7); all mourners comforted, perhaps not equally
The acceptable time and day of salvation is the martyr's procession under guard, a triumph with Christ over the powers (Isaiah 49:8; Colossians 2:15)
Give no offence, that the presbyterate or ministry be not blamed; commend yourselves in endurance, afflictions, necessities, straits, beatings (2 Corinthians 6:3-5)
The Lord's reward is in his hand to repay each by his works (Revelation 22:12)
translator_notes: 'the presbyterate or the ministry' (τὸ πρεσβυτέριον ἢ ἡ διακονία): Origen inserts 'the presbyterate' into 2 Corinthians 6:3. The pairing probably answers to the two addressees, Protoctetus the presbyter and Ambrose the deacon; English keeps the plain words.

The closing line blends Isaiah 40:10 and 62:11 ('his reward is with him') with Revelation 22:12 ('to repay each as his work is'); cited inline as Revelation 22:12, whose second half matches the wording.

Psalm 38:8 LXX = Psalm 39:7 English ('And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?' is the LXX sense; the Hebrew reads 'what do I wait for? my hope is in you'). Psalm 33:20 LXX = Psalm 34:19 English.
M reads 'καὶ νῦν'; Delarue 'νῦν δέ'. M has 'ἵν᾽ ὡς' where P and Delarue read 'καί'. English follows Koetschau (M).
title: Sharing Christ's sufferings and his comfort

english: Now let us show that we have desired knowledge for the sake of works that befit knowledge. Let every kind of purity be made plain in us: purity from every defilement whatever, in whatever sin it lies. As sons of a long-suffering God and brothers of a long-suffering Christ, let us be long-suffering in all that happens to us; for “a long-suffering man is great in understanding, but the faint-hearted man is utterly foolish” (Proverbs 14:29). If a man must commend himself “by the weapons of righteousness, for the right hand and for the left” (2 Corinthians 6:7), then, having commended ourselves “through glory” (2 Corinthians 6:8) without growing vain over it, let us now endure dishonour as well. And if we have lived in a way that deserved good report, and were well spoken of, let us now bear the ill report of the ungodly too.

Further, if we were admired as truthful by those who love the truth, let us now laugh when it is said that we have gone astray. In many dangers from which we were rescued, many people said that we were acknowledged by God; now let anyone who likes say that we are unknown, at a time when perhaps we are more fully acknowledged. So, bearing what happens to us, we are “disciplined but not put to death” (2 Corinthians 6:9), and we who rejoice look like those who grieve.
notes_covered: Show knowledge through fitting works; let purity from every defilement be plain (2 Corinthians 6:6)
Long-suffering sons of a long-suffering God (Proverbs 14:29)
Having been commended through glory and good report, endure dishonour and ill report; laugh at being called astray (2 Corinthians 6:7-8)
Once called acknowledged by God, now called unknown; disciplined but not killed, rejoicing while seeming to grieve (2 Corinthians 6:9-10)
translator_notes: The chapter walks through 2 Corinthians 6:6-10 (knowledge, purity, long-suffering, weapons of righteousness, glory and dishonour, ill report and good report, deceivers and true, unknown and well known, disciplined and not killed, sorrowful yet rejoicing). Only clauses quoted closely are cited inline; 'knowledge' and 'purity' (6:6), 'unknown ... acknowledged' (6:9) and the reversed 'we who rejoice look like those who grieve' (6:10) are left uncited as allusions.
'διὰ ἔργα' (accusative) is printed by Koetschau: 'for the sake of works'. A genitive ('through works') would give 'show by works that we desired knowledge'; English follows the printed case.
'ἀπὸ παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν ... μολυσμοῦ' is in M only (P and Delarue omit it); English follows Koetschau.
title: Through glory and dishonour alike

english: Paul says somewhere to those who had endured at the beginning, urging them to bear the second dangers, the ones that come for the word's sake, in keeping with the endurance they had shown before: “But remember the earlier days, when, after you had been enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings: at times you were made a public spectacle by reproaches and afflictions, and at times you became partners of those who lived in that state. For you also suffered with me in my bonds, and you accepted the plundering of your property with joy, knowing that you have a better possession, and a lasting one. So do not throw away your boldness, which has a great reward. For you need endurance” (Hebrews 10:32-36).

Let us too, then, now endure “a great contest” “of sufferings”, being made a spectacle “by reproaches and afflictions”, and accepting “with joy” “the plundering of” our “property”. For we are persuaded that we have a “better” “possession”: not earthly, nor even bodily, but one that is invisible and incorporeal. For we look not at “the things that are seen” (2 Corinthians 4:18), since we see that these are “temporary” and those “eternal”.
notes_covered: Paul urges those who endured at the start to bear second dangers for the word (Hebrews 10:32-36 quoted)
We too endure the contest, the public shame and the plundering of goods with joy
Our better possession is neither earthly nor bodily but invisible and incorporeal; we look to the unseen (2 Corinthians 4:18)
translator_notes: Origen's text of Hebrews 10:34 reads 'my bonds' (τοῖς δεσμοῖς μου; 'μου' is written above the line in M and lacking in P and Delarue) and has no 'in heaven' after 'possession' (P and Delarue add 'ἐν οὐρανοῖς'). English follows Koetschau.
The quotation ends at 'For you need endurance' (the first words of Hebrews 10:36); the citation keeps the range Koetschau gives.
Origen attributes Hebrews to Paul ('Φησί που ὁ Παῦλος'); kept as he says it.
title: A better and lasting possession

english: Some people do not consider the teaching about the demons: that, in order to stay in this thick air around the earth, they need the nourishment that comes from fumes, and so they keep watch wherever there is always the smell of burnt fat, and blood, and incense. Since these people make light of sacrificing as a matter of indifference, we would say this to them as well. If those who supply food to robbers and murderers and to barbarian enemies of the great king are punished as men who have wronged the commonwealth, how much more justly would those be charged who by sacrificing give food to the servants of wickedness, food that keeps them in the region around the earth; and above all if, having learned the words, “He who sacrifices to other gods shall be utterly destroyed, except to the Lord alone” (Exodus 22:20), they should sacrifice to the causes of the evils on earth.

And I think that for the sins committed by the demons as they work against human beings, those who fed them by sacrificing will be charged no less than the demons who did the evil work. For the demons and those who kept them on earth have, as it were, done the evils to human beings together, since the demons could not have lasted without the fumes and what are thought to be the foods suited to their bodies.
notes_covered: Some treat sacrifice as indifferent, not knowing that demons need the fumes of fat, blood and incense to stay in the air about the earth
Feeding the emperor's enemies is punished; feeding the servants of wickedness by sacrifice deserves heavier charge (Exodus 22:20)
Those who feed demons share the charge for the evils the demons work
translator_notes: 'ἐπιτηροῦσιν ὅπη κνῖσαι ...': Koetschau prints M's 'ὅπη' ('where'; P and Delarue 'ὅπου'); the OCR shows '0x xviooa'. English: 'they keep watch wherever there is always the smell of burnt fat'.
'the great king' (τοῦ μεγάλου βασιλέως) is the emperor; English keeps Origen's phrase.
Exodus 22:20 is 22:19 in the LXX numbering; the English verse is cited.
In P and Delarue the words 'τοῖς τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς κακῶν αἰτίοις' stand inside the Exodus quotation and the verb is 'θύειν'; Koetschau follows M ('θύοιεν' after the quotation). English follows Koetschau.
title: Sacrifice feeds the demons

english: Again, some suppose that names are a matter of convention and have no natural bond with the things of which they are names. They think it makes no difference whether one says, “I worship the first God”, or “Zeus”, or “Zen”; or whether one declares, “I honour and acknowledge the sun”, or “Apollo”; “the moon”, or “Artemis”; “the spirit in the earth”, or “Demeter”; and whatever else the wise men of the Greeks say. To them we must reply that there is also a very deep and recondite study of names. Whoever understands it will see that if names were a matter of convention, the beings that are called on, demons or other powers invisible to us, would not answer those who mean them and call them by names as though the names had simply been laid down. As it is, certain sounds and syllables, and names spoken with a rough breathing or a smooth one, with a long vowel or a short, bring those who are called, perhaps by some nature that we cannot observe.

If this is so, and names are not a matter of convention, then the first God must be called by no other name than those by which the servant [Moses] and the prophets and our Saviour and Lord himself name him, such as Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai, and again, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob; “for this”, he says, “is an eternal name and a memorial for generation after generation” (Exodus 3:15). It is no wonder if the demons carry their own names over to the first God, so that they may be worshipped as the first God. That is not the ancestral way of our servant, or of the prophets, or of Christ, “the fulfilment of the law”, or of his apostles. We have set these things out because we had to, so that no one may outwit us with clever arguments, or defile our reasoning even a little. We must attend to them with care, giving our opponents no opening for attack.
notes_covered: Some hold that names are conventional, so 'first God' or 'Zeus', 'sun' or 'Apollo', makes no difference
A deep study of names: demons answer to particular sounds, breathings and vowel lengths, so names are not mere convention
God is to be named only as Moses, the prophets and the Saviour name him: Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai, God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:15)
Demons transfer their names to the first God to be worshipped; this is not the ancestral way; give opponents no foothold
translator_notes: 'ὁ θεράπων' ('the servant') is Moses (Numbers 12:7; Hebrews 3:5, in Koetschau's apparatus); the name is supplied in brackets at its first use.

'πληρώματι νόμου Χριστῷ' ('Christ, the fulfilment of the law'): Koetschau compares Romans 10:4 ('Christ is the end of the law') and Colossians 1:19, 2:9; the wording matches none closely (Romans 13:10 has 'πλήρωμα νόμου' of love), so it is left uncited.

'(ἢ) ἄλλαι' is Koetschau's supplement (MP 'ἀλλά'); English follows it: 'demons or other powers'. Koetschau notes that 'νοοῦσιν' here means 'mean' (German 'meinen'), against Delarue's '(μὴ) νοοῦσιν'; English follows Koetschau: 'those who mean them'.
Exodus 3:15 as Origen quotes it lacks 'my' ('this is an eternal name'); English follows his wording.
title: Names are not mere convention

english: Further, a man also loves life once he has been convinced about the essence of the rational soul, that it has something akin to God. For both are intellectual and invisible, and, as the prevailing argument shows, incorporeal. And why did he who fashioned us plant in us a longing for godliness towards him and for fellowship with him, a longing that keeps some traces of the divine will even in those who have gone astray, if it were not possible and within reach for rational beings to lay hold of what they naturally long for? It is clear that, just as each of our members is made by nature to keep a certain affinity with something, the eyes with what is seen and the ears with what is heard, so the mind is made for what is intelligible and for the God who is beyond the intelligible.

Why then do we shrink and hesitate to put off the “corruptible body” that hinders us, that “weighs down the soul”, the “earthly tent” that burdens “the anxious mind” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15), to be set free from our bonds and to depart from the waves that go with flesh and blood? We would do it so that with Christ Jesus we may rest the rest that belongs to blessedness: contemplating the Word, the same, whole and alive throughout; being fed by him; grasping the richly varied wisdom in him; being stamped by Truth itself; and having our minds lit by the true and unfailing light of knowledge, so as to behold the things that by nature are seen through that light, with eyes enlightened by the Lord's commandment (Psalm 19:8).
notes_covered: The rational soul is akin to God: both intellectual, invisible and incorporeal
The Creator would not plant a longing for himself that cannot be reached; the mind is made for the intelligible and for God beyond it
Why hesitate to put off the body that weighs down the soul (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15) and depart from flesh and blood?
Rest with Christ: contemplating the Word, fed by him, stamped by Truth, eyes enlightened by the Lord's commandment
translator_notes: The first sentence ('Ἔτι δὲ καὶ φιλοζωεῖ ἄνθρωπος πεῖσμα λαβών ...') is translated as printed: 'a man also loves life once he has been convinced'. Koetschau notes that in M 'φιλοζωεῖ' seems corrected from 'φιλοζω ἢ'. Elsewhere in the work 'love of life' is a fault (ch. 40), so the sense here (love of true life?) is uncertain; a human should look at it.
Wisdom of Solomon 9:15 is cited on Koetschau's apparatus; Origen's words ('φθαρτὸν σῶμα', 'βαρῦνον ψυχήν', 'βρῖθον νοῦν πολυφρόντιδα', 'γεῶδες σκῆνος') plainly match it.
Psalm 19:8 (LXX 18:9, 'the commandment of the Lord ... enlightening the eyes') is my identification, not Koetschau's (he compares Ephesians 1:18); the wording matches.

Possible allusions left uncited: 'ἀναλῦσαι' (Philippians 1:23, 'to depart'); 'flesh and blood' (1 Corinthians 15:50 and others); 'the richly varied wisdom' (Ephesians 3:10); 'the true light' (John 1:9).
Koetschau adds '(ἐν) αὐτῷ' with Delarue; English follows: 'the wisdom in him'. M reads 'ἀληθινῷ' (Delarue 'ἀληθεῖ'): 'true light'.
title: The soul's kinship with God

english: Long ago we heard the words of Jesus, and for a long time now we have been disciples of the Gospel, and we have all built ourselves a house. But where we built it, whether we dug and went deep and built “upon the rock” (Luke 6:48), or “upon the sand” (Matthew 7:26) “without a foundation” (Luke 6:49), the present contest will show. For a storm has set in, bringing rain and rivers and winds, or, as Luke calls it, a flood. When these have burst against the house, either they will not be strong enough “to shake it”, and so the house will not fall, since it is founded “upon the rock”, Christ; or they will expose the rottenness of the building, which will collapse under the present occasion. May that be far from our buildings! For very great is the fall in denial, or, as Luke says, great is “the ruin” of the building without the foundation.

So let us pray that we may be likened “to a wise man who built his house upon the rock” (Matthew 7:24). Let the “rain” come against such a building from “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12), or the “rivers” of the principalities and powers that are hostile to us, or the harsh winds from “the world-rulers of this darkness”, or a flood of the spirits beneath the earth; and let them dash themselves against our building that stands “upon the rock”, so that, with the house not only not falling but not even being shaken at all, the powers at work may suffer at our hands rather than act. And let each of you say, as he strikes his adversaries, “So I box, not as one beating the air” (1 Corinthians 9:26).
notes_covered: We have long been disciples and have all built a house; the present contest will show whether on rock or sand
The storm (Luke's flood) either cannot shake the house founded on Christ the rock or exposes its rottenness; the fall in denial is great
Pray to be the wise builder; let the hostile powers dash themselves on the house and suffer rather than act (Ephesians 6:12)
Each should strike his adversaries: 'not as one beating the air' (1 Corinthians 9:26)
translator_notes: The chapter weaves Matthew 7:24-27 and Luke 6:48-49 together; one citation is given per quoted phrase where the wording is plainly from one Gospel. 'to shake it' and 'the ruin' are Luke 6:48-49 and 'founded upon the rock' Matthew 7:25; those short phrases are not cited separately.
'μεμαθητεύμεθα' ('we have been made disciples') is M's reading, printed by Koetschau; P and Delarue read 'πεπολιτεύμεθα' ('we have lived as citizens').
'ἑκάτερος ὑμῶν' ('each of you', i.e. both addressees) is Koetschau's correction ('ὑμῶν', against 'ἡμῶν' in MP and Delarue). '(μόνον)' is Delarue's supplement, printed by Koetschau.
title: The house built on the rock

english: And since “the sower went out to sow” (Matthew 13:3), let us show that our soul received “his seed” not as “those beside the road”, nor as “the rocky places”, nor as “the thorns”, but as the good earth. That the word of Jesus did not fall “beside the road” or “among the thorns”, as far as it rests with us, we will boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31). For we have understood what was said; that is why “the evil one” did not snatch away “what was sown in our heart” (Matthew 13:19). And that it was not sown “among the thorns” either, many will bear witness for us, seeing that neither “the care of this age” nor “the deceitfulness of riches” (Matthew 13:22) nor the pleasures of life have been able to hinder the word of God in our souls. It remains for people to be in doubt whether the word of God, as far as it rests with us, came “upon the rocky places” or upon the good earth. For affliction and persecution have come because of the word, and a time of great trial has set in, in which the one “sown upon the rocky places” is shown up, along with those who did not go deep and did not receive Jesus down to the depth of the soul; but the one who “understands the word” “bears fruit” and holds fast to the word to the end “with endurance”, yielding “a hundredfold”.

For we hear how Scripture presents those who, in a time “of affliction or persecution”, stumble after seeming to have received the holy teachings with joy, and who stumble because they have no root but believe for a season. According to Matthew it says, “But the one sown upon the rocky places, this is he who hears the word and at once receives it with joy; yet he has no root in himself but lasts only for a season, and when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, at once he stumbles” (Matthew 13:20-21). According to Mark: “These are the ones sown upon the rocky places, who, when they hear the word, at once receive it with joy, and they have no root in themselves but last only for a season; then, when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, at once they stumble” (Mark 4:16-17). According to Luke: “Those upon the rock are the ones who, when they hear, receive the word with joy; and these have no root; they believe for a season, and in a time of trial they fall away” (Luke 8:13). And teaching about those who bear fruit well, it says, “But the one sown upon the good earth, this is he who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields, one a hundred, another sixty, another thirty” (Matthew 13:23); or, “And those are the ones sown upon the good earth, who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold” (Mark 4:20); or, “But that on the good earth, these are the ones who, having heard the word with a noble and good heart, hold it fast and bear fruit with endurance” (Luke 8:15).

So, as the apostle says, since “you are God's field, God's building” (1 Corinthians 3:9), a “field” in the good earth and a “building” on the rock, let us stand unshaken against the storm as “God's building”; and as “God's field” let us pay no heed to the evil one, nor to the “affliction or persecution” that comes “because of the word”, nor to the care of this age or the deceitfulness of riches or “the pleasures of life” (Luke 8:14). Rather, despising all these, let us take up the spirit of wisdom that is free from care, and hasten to the riches that hold no deceit at all, and press on to the pleasures, if I may call them that, “of the paradise of delight”. In each of our hardships let us reckon that “the momentary lightness of our affliction is working for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, as we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen” (2 Corinthians 4:17-18).
notes_covered: The sower went out: show that our soul received the seed as good earth, not as road, rock or thorns
Not the road (we understood) nor the thorns (cares, riches, pleasures have not hindered us); persecution now tests whether rock or good soil
The rocky ground in Matthew, Mark and Luke (Matthew 13:20-21; Mark 4:16-17; Luke 8:13) and the good soil (Matthew 13:23; Mark 4:20; Luke 8:15)
God's field and building (1 Corinthians 3:9): stand unshaken, despise cares, press on to the paradise of delight; light affliction, eternal glory (2 Corinthians 4:17-18)
translator_notes: 'the good [earth]': Koetschau supplies '(γῆν)' after 'καλήν' from Matthew 13:23; bracketed. '(ἐκεῖνοι)' and '(οἱ)' in the Mark 4:20 quotation are Koetschau's supplements with Delarue, from the New Testament; translated without brackets because the quotation is otherwise exact.

'of the paradise of delight' (τοῦ παραδείσου τῆς τρυφῆς) is the LXX phrase of Genesis 3:23 (and 2:15), where the English Bible reads 'the garden of Eden'; left uncited inline, since the English verse does not have these words.
'the spirit of wisdom' may echo Ephesians 1:17, Isaiah 11:2 or Wisdom of Solomon 7:7 (Koetschau's apparatus); left uncited.
'we will boast in the Lord' alludes to 1 Corinthians 1:31 (Jeremiah 9:24); cited as 1 Corinthians 1:31.
The chapter ends inside 2 Corinthians 4:18 at 'the things that are not seen'; the OCR shows a stray 'Ἧ' after it, and a stray '[' before the first word; neither is text.
title: Rocky ground or good soil

english: Let us also know this: that what is said of Abel, killed by the murderous and unjust Cain, fits all whose blood has been shed unjustly. For let us consider that “the voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the earth” (Genesis 4:10) is said also of each of the martyrs, the voice of whose blood cries out to God from the earth. And perhaps, just as we were bought with the “precious blood” (1 Peter 1:19) of Jesus, when Jesus received “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9), so some will be bought with the “precious blood” of the martyrs; and the martyrs themselves will be exalted more than they would have been exalted had they become righteous but not borne witness.

For there is good reason why death in martyrdom is called, in a special sense, an exaltation, as is clear from the words, “If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself” (John 12:32). Let us too, then, glorify God, exalting him by our own death, since the martyr “will glorify God” by his own “death”. This too we have learned from John, who said, “He said this signifying by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:19).
notes_covered: What is said of Abel's blood applies to all whose blood is shed unjustly, and to each martyr (Genesis 4:10)
As we were bought with Jesus' precious blood, some will be bought by the martyrs' blood, and the martyrs more highly exalted (1 Peter 1:19; Philippians 2:9)
Death in martyrdom is properly called exaltation (John 12:32); let us glorify God by our death (John 21:19)
translator_notes: 'ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς' (second time) is Koetschau's text after Wettstein and Delarue; MP read 'ἐπί'.
'καὶ αὐτῶν πλέον ὑψουμένων' ('the martyrs themselves exalted more') is in M only (P and Delarue omit 'ὑψουμένων'); English follows Koetschau.
'bought ... with blood' may also echo Revelation 5:9 (Koetschau's apparatus); the inline citation gives 1 Peter 1:19 for 'precious blood'.

The play on 'ὑψόω / ὕψωσις' ('exalt / lifting up') joins the martyr's exaltation to John 12:32; 'exalted / exaltation' is used in Origen's sentences and 'lifted up' in the quotation, since English cannot carry one word for both.
title: The martyrs' blood cries out

english: These things I have dictated to you as far as I could, with such means as I had, and I pray that they may prove useful to you for the present contest. But if you, now above all, as men worthy to see more of the mysteries of God, grasp things greater and richer than these, and more effective for the task before you, and so despise these as childish and cheap, I too would pray for that on your behalf. For what lies before you is not that your cause should be accomplished through us, but that it should be accomplished somehow. And would that it might be accomplished through words more divine and wiser, surpassing all human nature, and through the wisdom of God.
notes_covered: Origen has dictated these words as best he could and prays they help in the present contest
If his readers, worthy of more of God's mysteries, find greater things and despise these as childish, he prays for that too
What matters is not that their cause be accomplished through him, but that it be accomplished, best by words and wisdom of God beyond human nature
translator_notes: Possible allusions left uncited: 'the mysteries of God' (Matthew 13:11, Luke 8:10); 'surpassing all human nature' (Philippians 4:7, 'which surpasses all understanding'), both 'compare' entries in Koetschau's apparatus.
'πρόκειται γὰρ ὑμῖν' ('lies before you') is M's reading; Delarue has 'ἡμῖν'. The text ends here in both M and P.
'λόγων καὶ σοφίας θεοῦ' is read as 'words ... and the wisdom of God', with the comparatives belonging to 'words'; 'of God' could also govern both nouns.
title: Words dictated for the present contest
